function:
def f(n: int, x: int, y: int, m: int) -> tuple:
    flag = x < y * m
    if flag:
        p = n // x
        q = p * y
        r = n - p * x
        u = r // m
        val = q + u
    else:
        u = n // m
        p = 0
        val = u
    d = {"used_rope": flag, "rope_units": p, "direct_torches": u}
    return val, d
description:
INPUTS: You start with four whole numbers: n, x, y, and m. Think of each of these as just a numeric value that you can add, multiply, divide, and compare with the others. There’s no list or text – just these four integers sitting in front of you. 

LOGICS: Alright, what you’re going to do first is decide whether to take the left path or the right path. To do that, multiply y by m. After you get that product, look at your x and ask: is x strictly smaller than that product? Write down that comparison result as a true-or-false marker called flag.  

If flag is true (meaning x < y · m):  
  1. You’re going to see how many full chunks of size x you can fit into n. To find that, do integer division of n by x (ignore any remainder) and call the result p.  
  2. Next, you want to figure out a temporary total by scaling p up by y. So multiply p times y and call that q.  
  3. Then find out what’s left over in n after removing those p chunks of size x. Calculate r = n – (p · x).  
  4. Now check how many full chunks of size m you can take out of the remainder r. Do integer division of r by m and call that u.  
  5. Finally, add that u to your earlier q to get your overall tally val = q + u.  

If flag is false (meaning x ≥ y · m):  
  1. You skip the step with p altogether and just figure out how many full chunks of size m you can fit into n. So do integer division of n by m and call that u.  
  2. Since you didn’t use any x-sized chunks, set p = 0.  
  3. Your overall tally val is simply the value you just got for u.  

At this point, regardless of which path you took, you have three numbers:  
  • flag (true or false),  
  • p (the count of x-sized chunks you used),  
  • u (the count of m-sized chunks you used),  
  • and val (the final total you calculated).  

Gather these into a little record called d, with three entries:  
  • used_rope: flag  
  • rope_units: p  
  • direct_torches: u  

Then you’re done. You return the pair: first the number val, and then the record d. 

OUTPUTS: In the end, you’ll have two things:  
1. A single integer val – that’s your combined total from whichever steps you took.  
2. A dictionary d with exactly three entries:  
   • used_rope: a true/false flag telling you which branch you ran.  
   • rope_units: the integer p, showing how many times you used the x-sized chunks (or 0 if you didn’t).  
   • direct_torches: the integer u, showing how many times you used the m-sized chunks.  

That pair (val, d) is exactly what the function would hand back if you did it by hand.

def f(n: int, x: int, y: int, m: int) -> tuple:
    flag = x < y * m
    if flag:
        p = n // x
        q = p * y
        r = n - p * x
        u = r // m
        val = q + u
    else:
        u = n // m
        p = 0
        val = u
    d = {"used_rope": flag, "rope_units": p, "direct_torches": u}
    return val, d

LOGICS: Alright, what you’re going to do first is decide whether to take the left path or the right path. To do that, multiply y by m. After you get that product, look at your x and ask: is x strictly smaller than that product? Write down that comparison result as a true-or-false marker called flag.  

If flag is true (meaning x < y · m):  
  1. You’re going to see how many full chunks of size x you can fit into n. To find that, do integer division of n by x (ignore any remainder) and call the result p.  
  2. Next, you want to figure out a temporary total by scaling p up by y. So multiply p times y and call that q.  
  3. Then find out what’s left over in n after removing those p chunks of size x. Calculate r = n – (p · x).  
  4. Now check how many full chunks of size m you can take out of the remainder r. Do integer division of r by m and call that u.

INPUTS: You’re working with three whole-number values called n, m, and val. Think of n and m as two integers you multiply together to get a workspace size, and val as another integer you want to check against that size and see how it divides into n or m. 

LOGICS: Okay, here’s how you do it step by step. First, what you’re going to do is multiply n by m and call that result x. So take your n and m, multiply them, and write down x = n * m. Next, set up a stats dictionary with two entries: early_exit starts at 0, and orientation_checks starts at 0. Now you need to see if val is bigger than x. So compare val to x. If val is greater than x, then set stats["early_exit"] to 1, and you’re done—you return False along with your stats. That ends the process early. If val is not greater than x (meaning val ≤ x), you keep going. At this point, you’re about to do your first orientation check, so add 1 to stats["orientation_checks"]. Now check whether val divides evenly by n: compute val modulo n and see if the remainder is zero. If the remainder is zero, that means val divides by n without leftover. In that case, figure out y by dividing val by n. Then check if y falls between 1 and m−1 inclusive—that is, make sure 1 ≤ y < m. If that condition holds, you return True and your stats right away. If either the modulo test failed or the y check failed, you move on. Next, you’re doing your second orientation check, so add 1 more to stats["orientation_checks"]. Now test whether val divides evenly by m: compute val modulo m and see if that remainder is zero. If it is zero, then compute z by dividing val by m. Then verify that z is between 1 and n−1 inclusive—so check 1 ≤ z < n. If that’s true, return True and stats. If not, or if the modulo wasn’t zero, then none of the checks succeeded, so you finally return False along with the stats dictionary. 

OUTPUTS: In the end you get two things: a True/False result and the stats dictionary. The True/False tells you whether either of those division-and-bounds checks passed. In stats, early_exit will be 1 if you quit right away because val was too big (otherwise it stays 0), and orientation_checks will be how many of those two division checks you actually performed (it will be 0, 1, or 2 depending on whether you exited early or passed one of the tests).

INPUTS: You’re working with three values called n, m, and k. All three of these are whole numbers (integers). 

LOGICS: First, lay out your workspace by writing down the three integer inputs n, m, and k. Next, create a stats dictionary with two entries named loop_iterations and segment_completions, both set to zero. Now, check whether k is equal to 1. If it is, what you’re going to do is multiply n and m to get your final value right away and stop—return that product together with your stats (which remain at zero). If k is not 1, you define a helper routine that processes a single integer x as follows:

- Start by setting a = 1 and b = 0.
- Then, for each y counting from 1 up to x (inclusive):
  - Immediately increase the counter loop_iterations in your stats by 1.
  - Set a temporary variable new_b equal to the current value of b.
  - Check if y is at least k:
    - If yes, increase the counter segment_completions in stats by 1, and add the value of a to new_b.
  - After that decision, overwrite b with new_b.
- Once you’ve gone through all y values up to x, the helper returns the final value of b.

After you’ve got that helper in place, go back to the main steps: call it with x = m and multiply its returned b by n; then call it again with x = n and multiply its returned b by m; finally, add those two products together to get your overall result. At that point, return that sum along with the stats dictionary, which has been accumulating counts during both helper runs. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two things: 1) a single integer—the sum of n times the helper’s result on m plus m times the helper’s result on n—and 2) your stats dictionary. In that dictionary, loop_iterations tells you how many times you ran through the counting loop in total, and segment_completions tells you how many times y met or exceeded k and triggered an addition to b.

LOGICS: First, you set up your workspace by creating an empty dictionary called mp to store links between numbers, then another dictionary called d with two counters 'find_calls' and 'path_updates' both set to 0, and finally an empty list called arr for the results. Now what you're going to do is define a helper named fn that takes a single number u. At the very start of fn, add 1 to d['find_calls']. Then check if u is not in mp. If it's not there, set mp[u] equal to u itself and return u right away. Otherwise, find the root: set a variable root equal to u and then, while mp[root] is not equal to root, set root equal to mp[root]. At this point, root holds the ultimate link. Next you're going to flatten the path: set current equal to u and then while mp[current] is not equal to current, do the following: first let nxt equal mp[current], then set mp[current] to root, then add 1 to d['path_updates'], and finally set current to nxt. When that loop ends, return root from fn. With fn in place, you move on to processing your list L. Now you need to go through each pair (x, y) in L in order. For each pair, figure out m by taking x plus y minus 1, then dividing that sum by y using integer division to drop any remainder, and then multiplying the quotient by y to get the smallest multiple of y that's at least x. What you do next is call fn on that m and call its output val. Immediately append val to arr. Then call fn again on val plus y, take that second output, and store it in mp at key val by setting mp[val] equal to that second output. That way you've set up the next link. You repeat exactly those steps for every (x, y). When there are no more pairs left, you're done. 

OUTPUTS: At the end you have arr, which is a list of integers (one entry per original pair in L), and d, a dictionary where 'find_calls' is the total number of times you entered fn and 'path_updates' is the total number of times you reassigned a link in mp during your path-flattening steps.

def f(n, A, B):
    from bisect import bisect_left
    lst = sorted(zip(A, B), key=lambda v: v[0])
    A = [u for u, _ in lst]
    B = [v for _, v in lst]
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    stats = {'improvements': 0, 'eliminations': 0}
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        dp[i] = dp[i - 1] + 1
        x, y = A[i - 1], B[i - 1]
        val = x - y
        j = bisect_left(A, val)
        option = dp[j] + 1
        if option < dp[i]:
            dp[i] = option
            stats['improvements'] += 1
            stats['eliminations'] += (i - 1) - j
    return dp[n], stats

LOGICS: What you're going to do is first set up two counters named loop_iters and adjust, both starting at 0. Now look at your integer n and ask: is n less than or equal to 0? If it is, you stop right there and you know your result will be 0, with loop_iters still at 0 and adjust still at 0. If n is not less than or equal to 0, the next thing you check is: is n exactly 1? If it is, you stop again, but this time your result is 6, and your counters are still loop_iters = 0 and adjust = 0.

If neither of those two quick checks applies (so n is greater than 1), you move on. What you do is compute a value called val by taking n, multiplying by 12, and then subtracting 3. Next, you set up a small workspace: put x = 0, y = val, and root = 0.

Now you begin a loop that keeps going as long as x is less than or equal to y. At the top of that loop, add 1 to your loop_iters counter. Then find the midpoint m by adding x and y together and dividing by 2, ignoring any remainder (integer division). After that, square m to get p (so p = m times m).

Next, compare p to val: if p equals val exactly, set root to m and break out of the loop entirely. If p is less than val, that means your midpoint squared is too small, so set root to m and then move your lower bound up by setting x to m + 1. Otherwise (meaning p is greater than val), your midpoint squared is too big, so move your upper bound down by setting y to m - 1. Then loop back and repeat: check x versus y, increment loop_iters, compute a new midpoint, square it, and adjust x or y or break if you hit the exact square.

When that loop finishes—either because you broke out on an exact match or because x climbed above y—do one more check: multiply root by itself and see if it's still less than val. If it is, that means you need to round up one more step. So add 1 to root and set adjust to 1. If root squared is not less than val, leave root and adjust alone (adjust stays 0).

Finally, take your root value, double it to get your final result, and you’re done. You’ll hand back that result number along with the two counters loop_iters (how many times you went through the while loop) and ceil_adjustments (which is 1 if you had to bump root up, or 0 if you didn’t). 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two things: first, a single number called result, which is twice the integer root you found; and second, a small dictionary of statistics where loop_iters tells you how many iterations of the loop you performed, and ceil_adjustments tells you whether you performed one final increase of root (it’s 1 if you did that, or 0 if you didn’t).

Now what you’re going to do is loop over each row index i from 0 to n-1. For each i, loop over each column index j from 0 to n-1. At each step, look at M[i][j]. If that entry is a dot ('.'), then figure out three values: A[j+1], A[j], and B[j]. Find the least among those three, then add 1 to it. Write that result into B at index j+1. Right after that, add that same value into val and add 1 to x. If the entry M[i][j] is anything other than a dot, set B[j+1] to zero and add 1 to y. After you finish all the columns j for this particular row i, swap A and B—so you treat the array you just filled (B) as the new A—then recreate B as a fresh list of zeros of length n+1. Next, go back and process the next row i. Keep doing this until you’ve covered every row. At that point, you’re done with the main loop. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two things: val, which is the total you accumulated from all the dot entries, and a dictionary with 'dp_updates' equal to x (the count of times you updated B because you saw a dot) and 'dp_resets' equal to y (the count of times you set a B entry back to zero because you saw something other than a dot).

def f(n, d, L, B):
    import heapq
    arr = [0] * n
    y = 0
    lst = []
    left = 0
    c1 = 0
    c2 = 0
    c3 = 0
    for i in range(n):
        while left < i and L[i] - L[left] > d:
            left += 1
            c1 += 1
        while lst and lst[0][1] < left:
            heapq.heappop(lst)
            c2 += 1
        z = 0
        if lst:
            t = -lst[0][0]
            u = t + d - L[i]
            z = u if u > 0 else 0
        if z > 0:
            c3 += 1
        arr[i] = B[i] + z
        y = arr[i] if arr[i] > y else y
        heapq.heappush(lst, (-(arr[i] + L[i]), i))
    return y, {'num_left_advances': c1, 'num_heap_pops': c2, 'num_non_zero_extensions': c3}

def f(n, d, L, B):
    import heapq
    arr = [0] * n
    y = 0
    lst = []
    left = 0
    c1 = 0
    c2 = 0
    c3 = 0
    for i in range(n):
        while left < i and L[i] - L[left] > d:
            left += 1
            c1 += 1
        while lst and lst[0][1] < left:
            heapq.heappop(lst)
            c2 += 1
        z = 0

    import heapq
    arr = [0] * n
    y = 0
    lst = []
    left = 0
    c1 = 0
    c2 = 0
    c3 = 0
    for i in range(n):

            left += 1
            c1 += 1
        while lst and lst[0][1] < left:

            c2 += 1
        z = 0
        if lst:

            z = u if u > 0 else 0
        if z > 0:

        arr[i] = B[i] + z
        y = arr[i] if arr[i] > y else y
        heapq.heappush(lst, (-(arr[i] + L[i]), i))
    return y, {'num_left_advances': c1, 'num_heap_pops': c2, 'num_non_zero_extensions': c3}

INPUTS: You have two inputs: an integer called n and a list called A that holds zero or more integers. 

LOGICS: Start by setting up two counters, sim_iters and bs_iters, both beginning at zero.  What you’re going to do next is define a little helper process called g that takes a number m.  When you run g with some m, do this: first set a working variable named val equal to m, and set another variable y to zero.  Then go through each item in A one at a time.  For each item, which we’ll call x, add 1 to sim_iters—that’s tracking each inner step.  Next, compute d by subtracting y from x.  If d is greater than zero, check if val is smaller than d.  If val is smaller than d, you immediately stop and say g returns False.  If val is at least as big as d, subtract d from val and continue.  If instead d is zero or negative, you take the negative of d (so you’re actually getting |d|), add that to val, and then if val ever grows larger than your original m, set it back down to m.  After dealing with d, set y to the current x and move on to the next element in A.  Once you’ve handled every element without returning False, g returns True.  Now, back in the main work: first check if n is zero or A is empty.  If either of those is true, you skip all the searching and simply return 0 along with your two counters.  If you do have data, set lo equal to 0 and hi equal to the largest number found in A.  Also set ans equal to that same hi.  Now you run a loop as long as lo is less than or equal to hi.  At the top of each loop, add 1 to bs_iters—this is tracking each binary‐search step.  Then figure out x by taking lo plus hi and dividing by two, dropping any fraction.  Call your helper g with that x.  If g comes back True, set ans to this x, and then shrink the high side by setting hi to x minus 1.  If g comes back False, move the low side up by setting lo to x plus 1.  Then repeat: check lo and hi again, bump bs_iters, compute a new midpoint, call g, and adjust lo or hi until lo exceeds hi.  When you exit the loop, you’re done.  You have your final answer in ans and you’ve collected counts in sim_iters and bs_iters along the way. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you return two things.  First is ans, the final number you settled on.  Second is a small dictionary with two entries: bs_steps shows how many times you went through that outer search loop, and sim_steps shows how many element‐by‐element steps you ran inside your helper each time you called it.

def f(L):
    from collections import Counter
    mp = {}
    d = Counter(L)
    A = sorted(d.keys())
    d2 = {}
    res = 0
    c = 0
    n = 0
    m = 0
    k = 0
    for v in A:
        tot = d[v] + c
        d2[v] = tot
        if tot > res:
            res = tot
        pairs = tot // 2
        k += pairs
        c = pairs
        n += 1
    x = A[-1] + 1 if A else 0
    while c > 0:
        tot = c
        d2[x] = tot
        if tot > res:
            res = tot
        pairs = tot // 2
        k += pairs
        c = pairs
        x += 1
        m += 1
    mp['unique_levels'] = n
    mp['carry_levels'] = m
    mp['merge_pairs'] = k
    return res, mp

INPUTS: You have one input called L, which is a list of numbers (integers) that may include repeats. 

LOGICS: Start by creating an empty dictionary called mp – that’s where you’ll stash your final statistics. What you’re going to do next is count how many times each number appears in L. To do that, set up another dictionary called d. Now go through L item by item: for each number, if it isn’t already a key in d, add it with a count of 1; if it is already there, add 1 to its count. When you finish, d maps each distinct number to how many times it showed up.

Next, grab all the keys from d and put them into a list called A. Then sort A in ascending order so you process your numbers from smallest to largest. Now create a third empty dictionary called d2 – you’ll use this to store new totals at each level as you work.

Before you start looping, set up five variables: res = 0 (this will track the highest total you ever see), c = 0 (this is your “carry” that moves from one level to the next), n = 0 (this will count how many original unique values you process), m = 0 (this will count how many extra carry-only levels you process after those), and k = 0 (this will keep a running total of all the pairs you form).

Now begin the first loop over each value v in your sorted list A:
 1. Figure out tot by taking d[v] (the count you recorded) and adding c (the carry from whatever happened at the last step).  
 2. In your d2 dictionary, store that tot under the key v.  
 3. If tot is larger than the current res, set res to tot.  
 4. Compute pairs by dividing tot by 2 and rounding down (that’s tot // 2 in code).  
 5. Add those pairs to k.  
 6. Set c to that same number of pairs – that becomes your carry for the next iteration.  
 7. Add 1 to n, since you’ve processed one more of the original unique numbers.

When that loop finishes, you may still have a leftover carry c. You handle that with a second loop. First, if A is not empty, set x to one more than the last element in A; if A is empty, just set x to 0. This x represents the next “level” beyond your original values.

Now, while c is greater than zero, do these steps over and over:
 1. Let tot = c.  
 2. In d2, store tot under the key x.  
 3. If tot exceeds res, update res to tot.  
 4. Compute pairs = tot // 2.  
 5. Add pairs to k.  
 6. Set c = pairs.  
 7. Add 1 to m, because you’ve just processed another carry-only level.  
 8. Increase x by 1 so the next level uses the next integer.

Keep going until c falls to zero, then you exit this while-loop. At this point you’ve built up all your intermediate values in d2 and tracked everything in your counters.

Finally, fill in mp with those three counters: set mp['unique_levels'] = n, mp['carry_levels'] = m, and mp['merge_pairs'] = k. Then you hand back two things: the final value of res and the dictionary mp. 

OUTPUTS: You’ll end up with a pair of values. The first is res, which is the maximum total you ever saw at any level. The second is the dictionary mp, which has three entries:  • unique_levels: the number of distinct values you processed in the first loop (n)  • carry_levels: the number of extra levels you ran in the second loop (m)  • merge_pairs: the grand total of all the half-pairs you formed across both loops (k)

def f(n, par, L, C, lst):
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for y in range(2, n+1):
        p = par[y]
        A[p].append(y)
    B = [0] * (n+1)
    for y, cnt in lst:
        if 1 <= y <= n and cnt > 0:
            B[y] += cnt
    H = [0] * (n+1)
    res = 0
    shipments_moved = 0
    warehouses_opened = 0
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    def dfs(x):
        nonlocal res, shipments_moved, warehouses_opened
        f_x = B[x]
        for y in A[x]:
            H[y] = H[x] + L[y]
            f_y = dfs(y)
            shipments_moved += f_y
            res += f_y * L[y]
            f_x += f_y
        if x != 1 and f_x * H[x] > C[x]:
            res += C[x]
            warehouses_opened += 1
            f_x = 0
        return f_x
    dfs(1)
    return res, {'shipments_moved': shipments_moved, 'warehouses_opened': warehouses_opened}

INPUTS: You have five things to lay out on your table. First, n is a single integer. Next, par is a list of length n+1 (indexes 0 through n) where each entry is an integer. Then L is another list of length n+1 of numbers, and C is also a list of length n+1 of numbers. Finally, lst is a list of pairs, and each pair has two numbers: y and cnt. 

LOGICS: Okay, let’s walk through every step as if you’re doing it by hand. First, you’re going to build a structure called A. What you do is draw out n+1 boxes labeled 0 up to n, and in each box you’ll collect a list of children. Start by writing an empty list in each box. (You’ll never actually put anything in box 0, so once it’s there you can safely ignore it.)

Now you need to fill those boxes. Go through y from 2 up to n. For each y, look at par[y] and call that p. Find box p in your A structure and write y into that box’s list. That just means you’re recording that y belongs under p.

Next, you’ll make B, a list of n+1 zeros. That’s B[0]=0, B[1]=0, …, B[n]=0. You won’t use B[0] again, so you can ignore it. Now take your lst of pairs. For each pair (y, cnt), check two things: y must be between 1 and n inclusive, and cnt must be greater than zero. If both are true, go to B[y] and add cnt to whatever is already there. If either check fails, do nothing for that pair.

After that, set up H as another list of n+1 zeros—H[0]=0, H[1]=0, …, H[n]=0. Notice right away that H[1] starts at zero, which is exactly what you want for the root. You’ll never touch H[0] again, so you can ignore that box too. On your paper, also write down three running totals: res = 0, shipments_moved = 0, warehouses_opened = 0.

At this point we’re going to explore the structure with a depth-first pattern. Imagine a procedure called dfs(x). Here’s exactly what to do when you enter dfs at a given x:

  Step 1: Start by setting a local variable f_x equal to B[x]. This is your current count of shipments at node x before you handle any children.

  Step 2: Look at A[x], the list of children of x. If that list is non-empty, take each child y in the order you put them in A[x], and do the following:
    a. Compute H[y] by taking H[x] and adding L[y]. Write that down in your H list at position y.
    b. Call dfs(y). When that call finishes, it will return a number f_y.
    c. As soon as you get f_y back, add f_y into your global shipments_moved counter.
    d. Multiply f_y by L[y], then add that product into your global res.
    e. Also add f_y into your local f_x, so f_x grows by whatever shipments bubbled up from child y.
  If A[x] is empty, you skip all of step 2 and move straight to step 3.

  Step 3: Now you’ve handled every child of x (or skipped if there were none). Check this condition: if x is not 1 (so x > 1) AND f_x multiplied by H[x] is strictly greater than C[x], then do these three things:
    a. Add C[x] into your global res.
    b. Add 1 into your global warehouses_opened counter.
    c. Reset your local f_x to zero (you’re disposing of any shipments at x).

  Step 4: You’re done with node x. Return the current value of f_x to whoever called dfs(x).

To run it for the whole structure, simply call dfs(1). Follow those four steps exactly at each node in the tree. When that completes, you’ll have your final values for res, shipments_moved, and warehouses_opened. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll end up with two things. First, a single number called res, which is the total you accumulated by moving shipments (that’s every time you added f_y * L[y] in step 2d plus each C[x] when you opened a warehouse in step 3). Second, a small dictionary with two entries: 'shipments_moved' is the total of all f_y values you added into shipments_moved, and 'warehouses_opened' is the total number of times you triggered the condition in step 3 and reset f_x to zero.

def f(n, par, L, C, lst):
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for y in range(2, n+1):
        p = par[y]
        A[p].append(y)
    B = [0] * (n+1)
    for y, cnt in lst:
        if 1 <= y <= n and cnt > 0:
            B[y] += cnt
    H = [0] * (n+1)
    res = 0
    shipments_moved = 0
    warehouses_opened = 0
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    def dfs(x):
        nonlocal res, shipments_moved, warehouses_opened
        f_x = B[x]
        for y in A[x]:
            H[y] = H[x] + L[y]
            f_y = dfs(y)
            shipments_moved += f_y
            res += f_y * L[y]
            f_x += f_y
        if x != 1 and f_x * H[x] > C[x]:
            res += C[x]
            warehouses_opened += 1
            f_x = 0
        return f_x
    dfs(1)
    return res, {'shipments_moved': shipments_moved, 'warehouses_opened': warehouses_opened}

def f(n, par, L, C, lst):
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for y in range(2, n+1):
        p = par[y]
        A[p].append(y)
    B = [0] * (n+1)
    for y, cnt in lst:
        if 1 <= y <= n and cnt > 0:
            B[y] += cnt
    H = [0] * (n+1)
    res = 0
    shipments_moved = 0
    warehouses_opened = 0
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    def dfs(x):
        nonlocal res, shipments_moved, warehouses_opened
        f_x = B[x]
        for y in A[x]:
            H[y] = H[x] + L[y]
            f_y = dfs(y)
            shipments_moved += f_y
            res += f_y * L[y]
            f_x += f_y
        if x != 1 and f_x * H[x] > C[x]:
            res += C[x]
            warehouses_opened += 1
            f_x = 0
        return f_x
    dfs(1)
    return res, {'shipments_moved': shipments_moved, 'warehouses_opened': warehouses_opened}

def f(n, arr):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    stats = {"recursive_calls": 0, "elements_processed": 0}
    def dc(x, y):
        stats["recursive_calls"] += 1
        if y - x + 1 <= 32:
            sm = 0
            mx = 0
            for i in range(x, y + 1):
                stats["elements_processed"] += 1
                val = arr[i]
                sm += val
                if val > mx:
                    mx = val
            return sm, mx
        m = (x + y) // 2
        sm_l, mx_l = dc(x, m)
        sm_r, mx_r = dc(m + 1, y)
        total = sm_l + sm_r
        maximum = mx_l if mx_l > mx_r else mx_r
        return total, maximum
    if n < 2:
        return 0, stats
    total, maximum = dc(0, n - 1)
    bound1 = total // 2
    bound2 = total - maximum
    result = bound1 if bound1 < bound2 else bound2
    return result, stats

def f(arr):
    A = sorted(set(arr))
    n = len(A)
    mp = {v: i+1 for i, v in enumerate(A)}
    B = [0] * (n + 1)
    comp_count = n
    upd_steps = 0
    sel_steps = 0
    def add(i, delta):
        nonlocal upd_steps
        while i <= n:
            B[i] += delta
            upd_steps += 1
            i += i & -i
    def kth(k):
        nonlocal sel_steps
        idx = 0
        bit_mask = 1 << (n.bit_length() - 1)
        while bit_mask > 0:
            sel_steps += 1
            t = idx + bit_mask
            if t <= n and B[t] < k:
                idx = t
                k -= B[t]
            bit_mask >>= 1
        return idx + 1
    res = []
    cnt = 0
    for x in arr:
        add(mp[x], 1)
        cnt += 1
        k = (cnt + 1) // 2
        pos = kth(k)
        res.append(A[pos - 1])
    stats = {'uniq_count': comp_count, 'update_steps': upd_steps, 'select_steps': sel_steps}
    return res, stats

description:
INPUTS: You start off with one thing called lst, which is simply a list of pairs of numbers.  Each pair has two entries: the first number we’ll call x and the second number we’ll call y. 

LOGICS: Okay, here’s how you do it step by step by hand.  First, count how many pairs are in lst and write that down as n.  Next, sort all those pairs by their second entry (y) in ascending order and call the result arr.  So now arr is your sorted list of (x,y) pairs.

Now you’re going to build a helper list A.  Set a constant INF equal to a very large number, 10 raised to the 18th power.  Then create A so that it has n+1 slots (index 0 up to index n) and fill every slot with INF.  After that, go to the very first slot, A[0], and overwrite it with 0.

You also need three counters before you begin looping: set m equal to 0, support_checks equal to 0, and dp_updates equal to 0.

Alright, now the main work.  You’re going to walk through each pair in arr one at a time, so pick the first (x,y), then the next, and so on.  For each pair do this:

  1.  You look at your current m.  You’ll loop h from that m value down to zero (so if m is 3 you check h=3, then h=2, then h=1, then h=0).

  2.  For each h, check whether A[h] is less than or equal to y.  In plain terms, compare the number stored in A at position h to the y from your pair.

     -  If A[h] is bigger than y, you do nothing and move on to the next smaller h.
     -  If A[h] is less than or equal to y, then you do three things:
         a.  Add 1 to your support_checks counter.
         b.  Compute a value val by taking A[h] and adding x to it.
         c.  Now compare that val to the current number in A at position h+1.  If val is smaller than A[h+1], then overwrite A[h+1] with val and add 1 to dp_updates.  Also, if h+1 is larger than your current m, update m so that m becomes h+1.

  3.  Once you’ve done that check for h=0, you’re done with this (x,y) pair and you move on to the next one in arr.

You keep repeating that inner h-loop for every pair until you run out of pairs in arr.  At that point, you have built up your final A values, your final m, and you’ve recorded how many times you did support_checks and dp_updates. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll report back two things.  First is m, the biggest h+1 you ever reached.  Second is a little dictionary of your two counters: “support_checks” is the total times you found A[h] ≤ y, and “dp_updates” is the total times you actually overwrote an entry in A.  That’s it — m plus the counts of those two activities.

LOGICS: Start by setting INF to a very large integer (10^18) and remembering that str2 is always 'hard'. Now create a list called arr2 with four entries: the first entry is 0 and the next three entries are INF, so arr2 = [0, INF, INF, INF]. Also make two counters called x and y and set them both to 0. Now you need to prepare a new temporary list called arr3 with four entries, all set to INF. Then you loop through j = 0, 1, 2, and 3 in turn. At each j, you compare ch with the j-th character of str2 (that is, str2[j]). If they match, here’s what you do: first, update arr3[j] by taking the smaller of its current value and arr2[j] plus v. Right after you do that, add 1 to your counter x. Next, check whether j+1 is still less than 4. If it is, update arr3[j+1] by taking the smaller of its current value and arr2[j], and then add 1 to your counter y. If ch does not match str2[j], you skip those two updates and simply update arr3[j] by taking the smaller of its current value and arr2[j]; that way you carry forward the previous value for stage j. Once you’ve done that for j = 0 through 3, you have a completely filled-in arr3. At that point, replace arr2 with arr3, and then move on to the next character in str1. INPUTS: You start with two whole numbers called n and m. Then you have two grids named matrix1 and matrix2. Each grid has exactly n horizontal lines (rows) and m vertical slices (columns). On each spot in those grids you see either a hash mark '#' or some other character. That’s all your inputs. 

LOGICS: Okay, here’s how you do it step by step by hand.  

1. First, set up your workspace:  
   – Create a list called A with m slots. Put a zero in every slot.  
   – Create another list called B with m slots, also all zeros.  
   – Make two counters: collisions = 0 and updates = 0.  
   – Finally, pick a variable val and set it equal to n.  

2. Now you’re going to fill A and B with bit patterns based on the two grids.  
   – For each column index j running from 0 up to m−1, do this:  
     • For each row index i running from 0 up to n−1, do these checks in order:  
       1) Look at matrix1[i][j]. If it’s a '#', then in slot A[j] you need to turn on bit number i. The way you do that by hand is: write down the current A[j] in binary, then flip the i th bit (counting from zero at the right) from 0 to 1. If you prefer arithmetic, compute 1 shifted left i times (that’s 1×2^i) and add it to A[j] using bitwise OR logic so that any existing bits stay set.  
       2) Next, look at matrix2[i][j]. If that’s a '#', do the same thing for B[j]: turn on its i th bit.  
     • When you finish all rows i for this column j, move on to the next j.  
   – At the end of this double loop, A[j] holds a binary pattern of which rows in column j of matrix1 had a '#', and B[j] does the same for matrix2.  

3. Now you’ll scan through each column again to count collisions and maybe update your val.  
   – For each column index j from 0 to m−1, do this:  
     a) Let x = A[j] and y = B[j].  
     b) Check if both x and y are nonzero. In plain terms, that means each one has at least one bit set. If both have bits turned on, that is a collision: add 1 to collisions.  
     c) Still inside that same collision case, find two positions u and v:  
        · To get u (the highest set bit in x): write x in binary without any leading zeros. Count how many bits that is; subtract 1 to get u. For example, if x in binary is 10110, that’s 5 bits, so u = 5 − 1 = 4.  
        · To get v (the lowest set bit in y): look at y in binary and scan from the rightmost bit toward the left until you find the first '1'. Count how many steps you moved from the rightmost position; that count is v. For example, if y looks like 10010, the rightmost '1' is in position 1 (zero-based), so v = 1.  
     d) Compute d = v − u − 1.  
     e) If d is strictly less than your current val, then do two things:  
        • Replace val with this new number d.  
        • Add 1 to your updates counter.  
   – If either x or y was zero, you skip steps b through e and just move on to the next column.  

4. When you’ve gone through every column j, you’re done with the work.  You now have your final val, plus two counters collisions and updates that you’ve been bumping along the way. 

OUTPUTS: At the end of all that, you’ll hand back two things:  
1) The number val, which is the smallest d you ever found when both A[j] and B[j] had bits set. If they never both had bits at the same time, val will still be n.  
2) A small dictionary of statistics:  
   • collisions: the total count of columns where both bit-patterns were nonzero.  
   • updates: how many times you discovered a new smaller d and changed val.

def f(n, arr, lst):
    parent = list(range(n+2))
    rem = [0] + arr[:]
    d = {'find_calls': 0, 'while_iters': 0, 'merges': 0}
    def find(x):
        d['find_calls'] += 1
        if parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = find(parent[x])
        return parent[x]
    A = []
    for x, val in lst:
        idx = find(x)
        rem_val = val
        while idx <= n and rem_val > 0:
            d['while_iters'] += 1
            if rem[idx] >= rem_val:
                rem[idx] -= rem_val
                rem_val = 0
                if rem[idx] == 0:
                    parent[idx] = find(idx+1)
                    d['merges'] += 1
                break
            rem_val -= rem[idx]
            rem[idx] = 0
            parent[idx] = find(idx+1)
            d['merges'] += 1
            idx = parent[idx]
        A.append(rem_val)
    return A, d

    parent = list(range(n+2))

        return parent[x]

    for x, val in lst:
        idx = find(x)

        while idx <= n and rem_val > 0:

                if rem[idx] == 0:

                break

            rem[idx] = 0
            parent[idx] = find(idx+1)
            d['merges'] += 1
            idx = parent[idx]
        A.append(rem_val)
    return A, d

def f(n, arr, lst):
    parent = list(range(n+2))
    rem = [0] + arr[:]
    d = {'find_calls': 0, 'while_iters': 0, 'merges': 0}
    def find(x):
        d['find_calls'] += 1
        if parent[x] != x:
            parent[x] = find(parent[x])
        return parent[x]
    A = []
    for x, val in lst:
        idx = find(x)
        rem_val = val
        while idx <= n and rem_val > 0:
            d['while_iters'] += 1
            if rem[idx] >= rem_val:
                rem[idx] -= rem_val
                rem_val = 0
                if rem[idx] == 0:
                    parent[idx] = find(idx+1)
                    d['merges'] += 1
                break
            rem_val -= rem[idx]
            rem[idx] = 0
            parent[idx] = find(idx+1)
            d['merges'] += 1
            idx = parent[idx]
        A.append(rem_val)
    return A, d

def f(n, A):
    prev = [-1] * n
    nxt = [n] * n
    st = []
    l_pops = 0
    for i in range(n):
        while st and A[st[-1]] <= A[i]:
            st.pop()
            l_pops += 1
        prev[i] = st[-1] if st else -1
        st.append(i)
    st.clear()
    r_pops = 0
    for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
        while st and A[st[-1]] < A[i]:
            st.pop()
            r_pops += 1
        nxt[i] = st[-1] if st else n
        st.append(i)
    total = n * (n + 1) // 2
    balanced = 0
    for i in range(n):
        x = i - prev[i]
        y = nxt[i] - i
        balanced += x + y - 1
    return total - balanced, {'left_pops': l_pops, 'right_pops': r_pops, 'balanced_subarrays': balanced}

  1. While st is not empty AND A at the index on top of st is strictly less than A[i], pop the top index off st and add 1 to r_pops.

Next, create another list named nxt that also has n slots but fill every slot with the number n. Then grab an empty list called st to use like a stack, and set a counter l_pops to 0.

  2. After that popping is done, if st is still not empty, look at its new top and write that index into prev[i]; if st is empty, write -1 into prev[i].
  3. Finally, push the current index i onto st.
Keep going until i has reached n-1.

At this point, clear out your stack st so it’s empty again. Now set up another counter r_pops and make it 0.

function:
def f(n, A):
    prev = [-1] * n
    nxt = [n] * n
    st = []
    l_pops = 0
    for i in range(n):
        while st and A[st[-1]] <= A[i]:
            st.pop()
            l_pops += 1
        prev[i] = st[-1] if st else -1
        st.append(i)
    st.clear()
    r_pops = 0
    for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
        while st and A[st[-1]] < A[i]:
            st.pop()
            r_pops += 1
        nxt[i] = st[-1] if st else n
        st.append(i)
    total = n * (n + 1) // 2
    balanced = 0
    for i in range(n):
        x = i - prev[i]
        y = nxt[i] - i
        balanced += x + y - 1
    return total - balanced, {'left_pops': l_pops, 'right_pops': r_pops, 'balanced_subarrays': balanced}

    prev = [-1] * n
    nxt = [n] * n
    st = []
    l_pops = 0
    for i in range(n):
        while st and A[st[-1]] <= A[i]:
            st.pop()
            l_pops += 1
        prev[i] = st[-1] if st else -1
        st.append(i)
    st.clear()
    r_pops = 0
    for i in range(n-1, -1, -1):
        while st and A[st[-1]] < A[i]:

            r_pops += 1

   - Create an empty dictionary named d.
   - Go through each item in your list L one by one. For each item:
     • If it’s not already in d, add it with a count of 1.
     • If it is already in d, add 1 to its existing count.

2. Find m (we’ll call this the first run count) and record how many checks you make in mex1_steps:
   - Set mex1_steps to 0 and set a variable x to 0.
   - Now, check d for x’s count:
     • If d has x and its count is at least 1, then:
         – Add 1 to mex1_steps.
         – Add 1 to x.
         – Repeat this check with the new x value.
     • The moment you see that d has no entry for x or its count is zero, stop the loop.
   - At that stopping point, whatever x is right now, call that m.

3. Find n (the second run count) and keep track with mex2_steps:
   - Reset x back to 0, and set mex2_steps to 0.
   - Do a similar loop:
     • While d has an entry for x with count of 2 or more:
         – Add 1 to mex2_steps.
         – Add 1 to x.
         – Keep repeating.
     • As soon as you see no entry or a count less than 2, exit the loop.
   - When you exit, whatever x is now, call that n.

4. Compute s:
   - Simply add m and n together and store that in s (so s = m + n).

5. Prepare to build your output list lst and count second-time assignments:
   - Make an empty dictionary called cache.
   - Create a new list called lst that has the same length as L, and fill every position with 1 for now.
   - Set a counter sec_assigns to 0.

6. Fill in lst based on how many times each value has appeared so far:
   - Go through L by index. For each position i (starting at 0) grab the value val = L[i].
   - Look in cache for val:
     • If val is not in cache yet, treat its count c as 0.
     • If it is in cache, use the stored count as c.
   - Now check c:
     • If c is less than 2:
         – In lst at position i, put the value (c + 1).
         – In cache set cache[val] = c + 1.
         – If c was exactly 1 (meaning this is your second time seeing val), add 1 to sec_assigns.
     • If c is already 2 or more:
         – In lst at position i, leave a 1 there (you do not change cache in this branch).

Now, the way this works is you define a helper called g that takes a single integer n and returns another integer. Here’s exactly how to run g by hand:

1. Every time you begin g with an input n, add 1 to sum_calls.  
2. Then add 1 to current_depth.  
3. If current_depth just became larger than max_depth, overwrite max_depth with the new current_depth.  
4. Check if n is already a key in your cache dictionary:
   - If it is, set your result res to cache[n].  
   - If it isn’t, you do this:
     a. If n is less than 10, simply let res = n.  
     b. If n is 10 or greater, turn n into its string form s, count how many characters are in s, divide that count by 2 (dropping any fraction) to get m, then split s into two parts: the first m characters and the rest. Call the integer value of the first part n1 and the second part n2.  
     c. Recursively run g on n1 to get a number, and run g on n2 to get another number, then add those two numbers together and call that res.  
     d. After you compute res in either step a or step b, store cache[n] = res.
5. Before you leave g, subtract 1 from current_depth.  
6. Finally, g returns res.

Once g is defined, set up another helper named h that takes two inputs a and b:

1. Call g(a) and call that result x.  
2. Call g(b) and call that result y.  
3. Compare x and y: if x is greater or equal, h returns x; otherwise it returns y.

With both helpers ready, you do the main flow:

2. Call h(x2, y2) and write down its outcome as v2.

def f(n, arr, lst):
    import heapq
    edge_count = 0
    push_count = 0
    pop_count = 0
    L = [0] * n
    for x, y in lst:
        edge_count += 1
        L[x - 1] += 1
        L[y - 1] += 1
    B = [val - 1 for val in L]
    h = []
    for i in range(n):
        if B[i] > 0:
            heapq.heappush(h, (-arr[i], i))
            push_count += 1
    res = []
    total = sum(arr)
    res.append(total)
    for _ in range(n - 2):
        neg_w, idx = heapq.heappop(h)
        pop_count += 1
        total += -neg_w
        res.append(total)
        B[idx] -= 1
        if B[idx] > 0:
            heapq.heappush(h, (neg_w, idx))
            push_count += 1
    return (res, {'edge_count': edge_count, 'push_count': push_count, 'pop_count': pop_count})

INPUTS: You have three pieces of data to start with: first, a single integer n; second, a list called arr that contains n numerical values; and third, a list called lst that contains pairs of integers (each pair has two numbers between 1 and n). 

LOGICS: Start by creating three counters named edge_count, push_count, and pop_count, and set each one to zero. Next, build a list called L with n slots and write a zero in each slot. Now you’re going to walk through every pair in lst one at a time. For each pair, call its two entries x and y. Each time you handle one pair, add 1 to edge_count. Then go to position x minus 1 in your L list and add 1 there. After that, go to position y minus 1 in L and add 1 there as well. That finishes processing that pair, so move on until all pairs are done. 

At this point, L holds a count in each slot. The next thing is to make a new list called B, also with n slots. To fill B, look at each slot in L in order from the first to the nth: take its number, subtract 1, and write the result into the corresponding slot in B. 

Now set up an empty list called h. You’ll treat h like a priority queue by always keeping it sorted so that the smallest first element in each pair sits at the front. After that, go through each index i from 0 up to n minus 1. For each i, look at B[i]. If B[i] is greater than zero, you create a pair whose first part is the negative of arr[i] (that is, -arr[i]) and whose second part is i, then insert that pair into h and re-sort h so the smallest pair leads. Every time you insert, add 1 to push_count. 

Now you have h initialized. Next, prepare your results list: call it res and start it empty. Then compute total as the sum of all the numbers in arr, and append total as the first item of res. 

Now you’ll do a loop exactly n minus 2 times. Each time around the loop, do these steps:
1. Remove the first pair from h (that means the pair with the numerically smallest first element, breaking ties by the second element). Call its parts neg_w and idx, and add 1 to pop_count.
2. Compute the positive weight by taking -neg_w, then add that number to your running total. After updating total, append the new total value to res.
3. Go to B at position idx and subtract 1 from that value.
4. Check if the new B[idx] is still greater than zero. If it is, insert the same pair (neg_w, idx) back into h, re-sort h, and add 1 to push_count.

Repeat these four steps until you have done them n minus 2 times. At that point you’re completely done with the processing. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you will have two things. First, res is a list of numbers showing the evolving totals (its length will be n-1). Second, you’ll have a small dictionary of statistics with three entries: edge_count tells you how many pairs you processed from lst, push_count tells you how many times you inserted a pair into h, and pop_count tells you how many times you removed a pair from h.

    edge_count = 0
    push_count = 0
    pop_count = 0
    L = [0] * n
    for x, y in lst:
        edge_count += 1
        L[x - 1] += 1
        L[y - 1] += 1
    B = [val - 1 for val in L]
    h = []
    for i in range(n):
        if B[i] > 0:
            heapq.heappush(h, (-arr[i], i))
            push_count += 1
    res = []
    total = sum(arr)
    res.append(total)
    for _ in range(n - 2):
        neg_w, idx = heapq.heappop(h)
        pop_count += 1
        total += -neg_w
        res.append(total)
        B[idx] -= 1
        if B[idx] > 0:
            heapq.heappush(h, (neg_w, idx))
            push_count += 1
    return (res, {'edge_count': edge_count, 'push_count': push_count, 'pop_count': pop_count})

        if y == b:
            lst2.append(x)

    lst2.sort()
    inf = 10**18
    i1 = bisect.bisect_right(lst1, b)
    r_obs = lst1[i1] if i1 < len(lst1) else inf
    l_obs = lst1[i1 - 1] if i1 > 0 else -inf
    i2 = bisect.bisect_right(lst2, a)

    u_obs = lst2[i2 - 1] if i2 > 0 else -inf
    d_r = (m - b) if r_obs == inf else (r_obs - b - 1)
    d_l = (b - 1) if l_obs == -inf else (b - l_obs - 1)
    d_d = (n - a) if d_obs == inf else (d_obs - a - 1)

def f(n, arr, Q):
    A = list(range(n+1))
    B = [0] * (n+1)
    C = [0] * n
    C[0] = 0
    find_calls = 0
    def g(x):
        nonlocal find_calls
        while A[x] != x:
            find_calls += 1
            A[x] = A[A[x]]
            x = A[x]
        find_calls += 1
        return x
    D = sorted(arr, key=lambda z: z[2])
    m = 0
    for x, y, val in D:
        ru = g(x)
        rv = g(y)
        if ru == rv:
            continue
        A[rv] = ru
        y = 2 * val
        B[ru] = max(B[ru], B[rv], B[ru]//2 + B[rv]//2 + y)
        m += 1
        C[m] = max(C[m-1], B[ru])
        if m == n - 1:
            break
    lst = []
    for y in Q:
        if y >= n:
            lst.append(0)
        else:
            lst.append(C[n-1-y]//2)
    return lst, {"find_calls": find_calls, "queries_count": len(Q)}

INPUTS: You start with three things: n, which is an integer count of how many numbers are in your list; m, another integer threshold; and A, which is a list of n numbers. 

LOGICS: What you're going to do is work through these numbers in a few clear steps.  

1. Sort A into a new list called B.  So you look at all the numbers in A and rearrange them in increasing order and call that sorted list B.  

2. Build a list C of the gaps between neighbors in B.  You go from i = 0 up to the second-to-last index of B.  For each i, you compute C[i] = B[i+1] minus B[i].  When you're done, C has one fewer element than B.  

3. Check if C is empty.  If B had 0 or 1 item, then there are no gaps and C is empty.  In that case you stop right here and you return out = 0, oversized_gaps = 0, query_steps = 0.  Otherwise, keep going.  

4. Find s, the size of your tree base.  Start with s = 1.  While s is less than the length of C, double it (s = s * 2).  When that loop finishes, s is the smallest power of two that’s at least as big as the number of gaps in C.  

5. Make an array T of length 2 * s and fill every entry with 0.  We’ll use this for a simple tree structure.  

6. Initialize a counter c1 = 0.  This will track how many gaps are "oversized."  

7. Now go through each gap in C by its index i (from 0 up to len(C) - 1):  
   - Let val = C[i].  
   - If val is greater than m, then compute t = floor((val - 1) / m).  That tells you how many extra pieces you need.  Put T[s + i] = t, and then add 1 to your oversized counter c1.  
   - Otherwise (val ≤ m), just leave T[s + i] = 0.  

8. Build the upper levels of the tree in T.  For each j from s - 1 down to 1 (in descending order), set T[j] = T[2*j] + T[2*j + 1].  You're summing two child slots into their parent.  

9. Prepare to do a full-range query.  Set another counter cnt = 0.  This will count how many times you enter the main loop of your query.  

10. Define the query process over an interval [l, r]:  
    a. Start res = 0.  
    b. Shift your interval into the tree level by doing l = l + s and r = r + s.  
    c. While l ≤ r, do these steps:  
       i.   Add 1 to cnt (this logs that you're about to inspect one or two tree slots).  
       ii.  If l is odd, add T[l] to res and then do l = l + 1.  
       iii. If r is even, add T[r] to res and then do r = r - 1.  
       iv.  After those checks, shrink the interval by doing l = l // 2 and r = r // 2.  
    d. When l passes r, exit the loop and return res.  

11. Finally, call that query with l = 0 and r = len(C) - 1.  Store its return value in out.  

12. You’re done.  Return out as your main result, and also hand back a little dictionary with two entries: 'oversized_gaps': c1 and 'query_steps': cnt. 

OUTPUTS: At the very end you get two things:  

• out: a single integer equal to the result of summing across the whole range of T according to the rules above.  
• A dictionary with two stats:  
   – 'oversized_gaps' is the count c1 of how many gaps in C exceeded m.  
   – 'query_steps' is the count cnt of how many times you entered the while-loop in the query routine.

INPUTS: You have two whole numbers called n and k, and you have a list named lst that contains n whole numbers. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is walk through a few phases by hand:

1) First, write down a big number M = 1000000007. Then create three counters named c1, c2, and c3, and set them all to zero.

2) Now check this: look at your numbers n and k. If either one is zero, stop right here. Your main output is zero, and c1, c2, c3 stay at zero. If both are positive, move to the next step.

3) Next, find m, the maximum value in your list. To do that, start with m = 0. Go through each item x in lst: if x is larger than your current m, replace m with x. After you finish, m holds the largest number.

4) At this point, create an array A with slots indexed from 0 up to m. Fill every slot in A with zero. Then, go through each x in lst again: for each one, look at slot A[x] and add 1 to it.

5) Now you’ll build another array B with slots 0 to m, all starting at zero. What you do is: for x running from 1 up to m, look at every multiple y of x (so y = x, 2·x, 3·x, … as long as y ≤ m). For each such y, add the value in A[y] into B[x]. Each time you do that addition, add 1 to counter c1.

6) Next, set size = n. Create two more arrays C and D, each with slots 0 to size, all initialized to 1. To fill C, run x from 1 up to size: multiply the previous slot C[x–1] by x, then reduce that product modulo M, and write it into C[x]. After each multiplication and reduction, add 1 to c2.

7) Once C is ready, you fill D. First compute D[size] as the modular inverse of C[size] modulo M—i.e. take C[size] to the power of M–2, reducing modulo M at each step (you can use repeated-squaring on paper). Then run x down from size to 1: multiply D[x] by x, reduce modulo M, and store it into D[x–1]. After each of those multiplications, add 1 to c2.

8) Now you have everything needed for combination. Whenever you want comb(n_, k_), first check: if k_ < 0 or k_ > n_, then comb(n_, k_) is 0. Otherwise, multiply C[n_] by D[k_], then by D[n_–k_], reducing modulo M after each multiplication.

9) Next, create an array E with slots 0 to m, all set to zero. Now work x from m down to 1:
   • First set E[x] = comb(B[x], k).
   • Then to correct for overcounts, run through every multiple y of x that’s bigger than x (so y = 2·x, 3·x, … ≤ m). For each such y, subtract E[y] from E[x]. If that makes E[x] negative, add M to bring it back into the 0 to M–1 range. After each subtraction, add 1 to c3.

10) When the loop finishes, your main result is the number held in E[1]. That completes the process. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two things: 1) a single number, which is the value stored in E[1], and 2) a small dictionary of your three counters:  - “divisor_multiples_ops” (that’s c1, the count of additions you did when building B)  - “factorial_mults” (that’s c2, the count of multiplications you did in arrays C and D)  - “dp_exclusions” (that’s c3, the count of subtractions you did when adjusting E)

If n is smaller than m, move on: compute lim by doubling m (so lim = m * 2). Now create two sets: call the first one st1 and put the single value n into it; call the second one st2 and put m into it. At the same time, make two dictionaries: d1 maps n to 0, and d2 maps m to 0.  

Now go into a loop that runs while st1 is not empty. Inside that loop, the very first thing is to compare the sizes of st1 and st2. If st1 has more items than st2, swap the contents of st1 with st2, and swap d1 with d2 too. After you do that swap, add 1 to stats['swaps'].  

Right after handling a possible swap, you’re starting a new search level—so add 1 to stats['levels']. Then create an empty set called st3; this will collect the next wave of values. Now, for each element x in st1, do the following: look up x in d1 and call that number val. Then consider two candidate values for y: one is x minus 1, the other is x times 2. For each of those y’s, first check that y is at least 0 and at most lim, and also make sure y is not already a key in d1. If all that is true, then check if y is already in the other dictionary, d2. If you find y in d2, you’ve met in the middle: add 1 to stats['nodes'], compute your final result as val + 1 + d2[y], and immediately return that result along with your stats. If y is not in d2, then record y in this dictionary by setting d1[y] = val + 1, add y into your set st3, and also add 1 to stats['nodes'].

LOGICS: Alright, here’s exactly how you do it by hand. First, get a piece of paper and write down two things: a counter named gcd_ops and set it to 0, and a list named res that starts out empty. That gcd_ops is going to track every time you compute a greatest common divisor.

Now you’re going to handle each sub-list in L one at a time. So you say: “Okay, I have L, and it contains n small lists. I’ll pull out the first sub-list and call it arr, then the second, then the third, all the way through the nth.” Do this in order.

For each arr, follow these steps:
1. Figure out m, the number of items in arr. You can count them one by one. That count is m.
2. Next to your page, write down a fresh variable ans and set that to 0. ans will collect a running total for this specific arr.
3. Also write down a dictionary called prev; at the very start for this arr, prev is empty—no keys, no values.
4. Now here’s the key loop: you’re going to look at every consecutive pair inside arr. Remember that the first element is arr[0], the second is arr[1], and so on up through arr[m-1]. So you start your index i at 1 and go up to i = m−1. For each index i, do the following:
   a. Compute the difference d by subtracting arr[i−1] from arr[i], then taking the absolute value so it’s never negative.
   b. Create a new dictionary called curr. Right away, put one entry into curr using the difference you just found: set curr[d] = 1. That accounts for the subarray of length one that ends at position i.
   c. Now you look inside prev. For every entry there, you have a key g and a count cnt. For each of those entries:
      - First, add 1 to gcd_ops—because you are about to do a gcd calculation.
      - Then compute the greatest common divisor of g and d by hand; call that result ng.

def f(n, m, x, y, lst):
    import heapq
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for a, b, val, lst2 in lst:
        lst2 = sorted(lst2)
        A[a].append((b, val, lst2))
    INF = float('inf')
    arr = [INF] * (n+1)
    arr[x] = 0
    pq = [(0, x)]
    def h(lst2, val2):
        i = 0
        j = len(lst2) - 1
        res = None
        while i <= j:
            k = (i + j) // 2
            if lst2[k] >= val2:
                res = lst2[k]
                j = k - 1
            else:
                i = k + 1
        return res
    c1 = 0
    c2 = 0
    c3 = 0
    while pq:
        t, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        c2 += 1
        if t > arr[u]:
            continue
        if u == y:
            break
        for v, val, lst2 in A[u]:
            c1 += 1
            dt = h(lst2, t)
            if dt is None:
                continue
            at = dt + val
            if at < arr[v]:
                arr[v] = at
                c3 += 1
                heapq.heappush(pq, (at, v))
    res = arr[y] if arr[y] != INF else -1
    return res, {'binary_search_calls': c1, 'heap_extractions': c2, 'edge_relaxations': c3}

Next, you go through every entry in lst one by one: for each entry, unpack it into a, b, val, and lst2. Then sort lst2 in ascending order. Once it’s sorted, go to A at position a and append the triple (b, val, lst2) there. That way you’ve grouped all your outgoing pieces by their a index.

At this point you have A set up. Now you need to define a special large value INF to stand for infinity – just a number bigger than any you’ll calculate. Create another list called arr of length n+1 and fill every position with INF. Then set arr[x] to 0, because you’re starting at index x with zero cost.

Now you need to prepare a min-heap named pq. Start by putting exactly one pair into it: (0, x), where 0 is the current cost t and x is the current index u. At the same time, initialize three counters to zero: c1 (to count how many times you search in lst2), c2 (to count how many times you pull from the heap), and c3 (to count how many times you update arr and push a new pair).

Next, define a helper routine h(lst2, val2) that finds the smallest number in lst2 that’s at least val2 by doing a manual binary search. Set i to 0 and j to len(lst2)−1, and let res start as None. While i ≤ j, compute k as the integer midpoint (i+j)//2. If lst2[k] ≥ val2, store lst2[k] in res and move j down to k−1. Otherwise move i up to k+1. When the loop ends, return res (it’ll be either your found number or None).

Now start the main loop: while pq isn’t empty, remove the pair with the smallest cost, naming those t and u, and add 1 to c2. First check if t > arr[u]: if it is, do a continue because you’ve already got a better way to u. Next check if u == y: if so, break out of the loop entirely since you’ve reached your target index y.

If you haven’t broken out, go through each triple stored in A[u]. For each one unpack it into v, val, and lst2, then immediately add 1 to c1 because you’re about to search in lst2. Call h(lst2, t) and call its result dt. If dt is None, do a continue to skip to the next outgoing triple. Otherwise compute at = dt + val. If at < arr[v], then you’ve found a better cost to reach v: set arr[v] = at, add 1 to c3, and push the pair (at, v) onto pq. Then carry on with the next triple in A[u].

You repeat that until either the heap is empty or you broke out because u == y. At that point, check arr[y]: if it’s still INF, set your final result res to -1; otherwise set res to arr[y]. Then you’re done – you return res plus a dictionary with your three counters.

def f(n, m, x, y, lst):
    import heapq
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for a, b, val, lst2 in lst:
        lst2 = sorted(lst2)
        A[a].append((b, val, lst2))
    INF = float('inf')
    arr = [INF] * (n+1)
    arr[x] = 0
    pq = [(0, x)]
    def h(lst2, val2):
        i = 0
        j = len(lst2) - 1
        res = None
        while i <= j:
            k = (i + j) // 2
            if lst2[k] >= val2:
                res = lst2[k]
                j = k - 1
            else:
                i = k + 1
        return res
    c1 = 0
    c2 = 0
    c3 = 0
    while pq:
        t, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        c2 += 1
        if t > arr[u]:
            continue
        if u == y:
            break
        for v, val, lst2 in A[u]:
            c1 += 1
            dt = h(lst2, t)
            if dt is None:
                continue
            at = dt + val
            if at < arr[v]:
                arr[v] = at
                c3 += 1
                heapq.heappush(pq, (at, v))
    res = arr[y] if arr[y] != INF else -1
    return res, {'binary_search_calls': c1, 'heap_extractions': c2, 'edge_relaxations': c3}

def f(n, m, x, y, lst):
    import heapq
    A = [[] for _ in range(n+1)]
    for a, b, val, lst2 in lst:
        lst2 = sorted(lst2)
        A[a].append((b, val, lst2))
    INF = float('inf')
    arr = [INF] * (n+1)
    arr[x] = 0
    pq = [(0, x)]
    def h(lst2, val2):
        i = 0
        j = len(lst2) - 1
        res = None
        while i <= j:
            k = (i + j) // 2
            if lst2[k] >= val2:
                res = lst2[k]
                j = k - 1
            else:
                i = k + 1
        return res
    c1 = 0
    c2 = 0
    c3 = 0
    while pq:
        t, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        c2 += 1
        if t > arr[u]:
            continue
        if u == y:
            break
        for v, val, lst2 in A[u]:
            c1 += 1
            dt = h(lst2, t)
            if dt is None:
                continue
            at = dt + val
            if at < arr[v]:
                arr[v] = at
                c3 += 1
                heapq.heappush(pq, (at, v))
    res = arr[y] if arr[y] != INF else -1
    return res, {'binary_search_calls': c1, 'heap_extractions': c2, 'edge_relaxations': c3}

So you create a little tally sheet called B, where each unique number from A gets its own line and you write down its count. Next, write down all the unique numbers you’ve tallied, in order from smallest to largest—call that sorted strip of numbers lst. Then you look at the very last number in lst and call it n; that’s just the biggest number you have.

Now grab four blank counters and put them on your sheet: sum_trials = 0, pointer_iterations = 0, matches_found = 0, and res = 0. These will track what you do as you go.

What you’re going to do now is test every possible target sum x from 2 up to 2·n. So you start with x = 2. Each time you begin a new x, immediately add 1 to sum_trials—that’s keeping count of how many x’s you’ve tried.

After that, you’re looking for pairs of numbers from lst that add up exactly to this x. So set another counter called pairs = 0. Then place two markers: one at the start of lst (call its position i = 0) and one at the end of lst (call its position j = length of lst minus 1).

Now you do this dance while i is not past j (so while i ≤ j):
  • First thing inside the loop, add 1 to pointer_iterations. That’s marking every time you compare a pair.  
  • Then look at the numbers under those two markers: call the left number v1 = lst[i] and the right number v2 = lst[j].  
  • Add them together to get s = v1 + v2.  
  • If s is less than x, that means even the biggest v2 paired with v1 isn’t enough, so move your left marker one step to the right by doing i = i + 1.  
  • Otherwise, if s is greater than x, even the smallest v1 with v2 is too big, so move your right marker one step to the left by doing j = j - 1.  
  • Otherwise, s exactly equals x, which is what you want:

      – If your left marker and right marker are on different entries (i < j), you can pair each copy of the smaller with each copy of the bigger, but limited by whichever count is smaller. So do pairs = pairs + min(B[v1], B[v2]).

INPUTS: You start with three things: 1) a single integer n, 2) a list A containing n numbers, and 3) a list Q where each item is itself three numbers (we’ll call them a, b, c in each query). 

LOGICS: Alright, let’s walk through every step as if we’re on the phone together.  

1. Lay out your inputs  
   - You’ve got n (just a single number).  
   - You’ve got A, a list of exactly n numbers, which we’ll refer to by positions 0 through n−1.  
   - You’ve got Q, a list of query triples, each triple written (a, b, c).  

2. Build a sorted list of unique values from A, call it U  
   - Go through A and jot down each distinct number on a scratch pad—no repeats.  
   - Once you’ve collected each distinct entry, sort those entries in ascending order.  Call that sorted list U.  

3. Record m, the length of U  
   - Count how many entries you have in U; that count is m.  

4. Create a mapping d from each value in U to a 1-based index  
   - Look at U[0], give it the label 1; look at U[1], give it label 2; … up to U[m−1] getting label m.  
   - On paper you now have pairs (value → its label). That’s your d.  

5. Compute mx, the maximum size for our working arrays  
   - Figure out how many bits it takes to write m in binary (that’s the bit_length of m).  
   - Add 2 to that bit_length.  
   - Multiply the result by n.  
   - Add 5.  
   - The final sum is mx.  

6. Allocate and initialize arrays and counters  
   - Create three arrays called B, C, S, each with indices from 0 up to mx−1, and fill every entry with 0.  
   - Create another array called roots with indices 0 through n, fill every entry with 0.  
   - On your sheet, note three counters: sz = 0, u_calls = 0, q_calls = 0.  

7. Define the update process (we’ll call it whenever we insert one more label)  
   When you say update(p, l_, r_, v):  
   a. Add 1 to u_calls.  
   b. Add 1 to sz.  Let cur = the new value of sz.  
   c. Copy old slots into the new one:  
      - B[cur] = B[p]  
      - C[cur] = C[p]  
      - S[cur] = S[p] + 1  
   d. If l_ is less than r_, then:  
      i.  Compute mid = floor((l_ + r_) / 2)  
      ii. If v ≤ mid, do a recursive update on the left side:  
          • Call update(B[p], l_, mid, v), get back some index, and store it into B[cur].  
         Else (v > mid), do a recursive update on the right side:  
          • Call update(C[p], mid+1, r_, v), get back some index, and store it into C[cur].  
   e. Return cur.  

8. Define the query process (we’ll call it to answer one (a,b,c) query)  
   When you say query(p, q, l_, r_, k):  
   a. Add 1 to q_calls.  
   b. If l_ equals r_, return l_ immediately.  
   c. Otherwise, compute mid = floor((l_ + r_) / 2).  
   d. Compute cnt = S[B[q]] − S[B[p]].  
   e. If k ≤ cnt, go left:  
      • Return query(B[p], B[q], l_, mid, k).  
      Else, go right:  
      • Return query(C[p], C[q], mid+1, r_, k − cnt).  

9. Build up your versions step by step  
   - For each i from 1 up to n (inclusive):  
     • Look at the previous version index roots[i−1].  
     • Compute v = d[A[i−1]] (that’s the label of your i-th element).  
     • Call update(roots[i−1], 1, m, v).  
     • The result is a new index; store it in roots[i].  

10. Answer each query in Q  
    - Start with an empty list called res.  
    - For each triple (a, b, c) in Q in order:  
      • Call query(roots[a−1], roots[b], 1, m, c); store the returned index as idx.  
      • Look up the real number U[idx−1] in your U list.  
      • Append U[idx−1] to res.  

11. Wrap up  
    - At this point your list res holds one number per query, in the same order as Q.  
    - Your counters u_calls and q_calls record how many times you did update and query, respectively.  

That’s it—follow those steps in order and you’ll end up with exactly the same results as the code. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll have two things:  
1) A list called res that contains one number for each query in Q—those are your final results in order.  
2) A small dictionary with two entries:  
   • "update_calls": the total count of how many times you entered the update process (that’s u_calls).  
   • "query_calls": the total count of how many times you entered the query process (that’s q_calls).  
Those three items together are exactly what the function would return.

def f(arr, m):
    x = 0
    y = 0
    n = len(arr)
    if m >= n:
        return 0, {"cost_calls": x, "dp_updates": y}
    A = [0] + sorted(arr)
    B = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        B[i] = B[i - 1] + A[i]
    def g(i, j):
        nonlocal x
        x += 1
        mid = (i + j) // 2
        v1 = A[mid] * (mid - i + 1) - (B[mid] - B[i - 1])
        v2 = (B[j] - B[mid]) - A[mid] * (j - mid)
        return v1 + v2
    INF = 10**18
    C = [INF] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        C[i] = g(1, i)
        y += 1
    C[0] = 0
    y += 1
    for t in range(2, m + 1):
        D = [INF] * (n + 1)
        for i in range(1, t):
            D[i] = 0
            y += 1
        def h(l, r, optl, optr):
            nonlocal y
            if l > r:
                return
            mid = (l + r) // 2
            best = INF
            opt = -1
            limit = min(optr, mid - 1)
            for j in range(optl, limit + 1):
                val = C[j] + g(j + 1, mid)
                if val < best:
                    best = val
                    opt = j
            D[mid] = best
            y += 1
            h(l, mid - 1, optl, opt)
            h(mid + 1, r, opt, optr)
        h(t, n, t - 1, n - 1)
        C = D
    return C[n], {"cost_calls": x, "dp_updates": y}

def f(str1: str, str2: str) -> tuple[int, dict]:
    n = len(str1)
    A = [(int(str2[i]) - int(str1[i])) % 10 for i in range(n)]
    INF = float('inf')
    B = [[[INF] * 10 for _ in range(10)] for __ in range(n + 1)]
    B[0][0][0] = 0
    states_processed = 0
    updates = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for x in range(10):
            for y in range(10):
                c = B[i][x][y]
                if c == INF:
                    continue
                states_processed += 1
                need = (A[i] - x) % 10
                nr = (y + need) % 10
                nl = need
                if B[i + 1][nr][nl] > c + need:
                    B[i + 1][nr][nl] = c + need
                    updates += 1
                dec = (10 - need) % 10
                nr2 = (y - dec) % 10
                nl2 = (-dec) % 10
                if B[i + 1][nr2][nl2] > c + dec:
                    B[i + 1][nr2][nl2] = c + dec
                    updates += 1
    res = B[n][0][0]
    out = res if res < INF else -1
    return out, {"states_processed": states_processed, "updates": updates}

INPUTS: Two text strings str1 and str2 of equal length n, each made up of digit characters; a list A of length n containing integers between 0 and 9; a three-dimensional table B with dimensions (n+1)×10×10 holding numeric values; and two integer counters states_processed and updates. 

LOGICS: Start by figuring out n as the length of str1. Next, create an empty list called A. Now you’re going to fill that list by going through each position i from 0 up to n minus 1. At each i, take the character at position i in str2 and convert it to an integer, then take the character at the same position in str1 and convert that to an integer. Subtract the str1 number from the str2 number, then adjust it by adding or subtracting 10 until it falls into the range 0 through 9. Record that result in A at position i. Once you’ve done this for every i, A is a list of n numbers between 0 and 9. After that, define a symbol INF to stand for a huge number, effectively ‘infinity’. On paper you can just write INF or use a large number you know you’ll never beat. Now you need to set up a three-dimensional table called B. Imagine there are n+1 layers, and each layer is a 10×10 grid of cells. Fill every cell in every layer with INF. Label the layers from 0 up to n, and label the rows and columns in each layer from 0 through 9. After that, go to the cell at layer 0, row 0, column 0 and overwrite it with 0. Next, create two counters named states_processed and updates, and set them both to zero. At this point, you begin the main processing. For each layer index i going from 0 up to n minus 1, do the following. First you look at layer i in B. Then you loop through every possible row index x from 0 through 9, and for each x you loop through every column index y from 0 through 9. For each pair (x,y), read the value c in B at layer i, row x, column y. If c is equal to INF, skip the rest of the steps for this pair and move on to the next (y or x). If c is not INF, add 1 to your states_processed counter. Now calculate need as A[i] minus x, then adjust that result by adding or subtracting 10 until it falls between 0 and 9. That is need = (A[i] - x) modulo 10. Next you handle two options. First option: call it the forward action. Calculate nr as y plus need, then adjust by subtracting 10 if it’s 10 or more so it stays between 0 and 9. Then set nl equal to need. Now look at the cell in the next layer, B at layer i+1, row nr, column nl. If that cell currently holds a number bigger than c plus need, overwrite it with c plus need and add 1 to updates. Second option: call it the reverse action. Figure out dec by subtracting need from 10, then adjust by subtracting 10 if it’s 10 or more, giving a number between 0 and 9. That is dec = (10 - need) modulo 10. Compute nr2 by subtracting dec from y, then adjust by adding 10 if it becomes negative, so nr2 stays in 0 through 9. Compute nl2 by taking minus dec, then if that is negative add 10 so it’s also between 0 and 9. Now check B at layer i+1, row nr2, column nl2. If that value is bigger than c plus dec, overwrite it with c plus dec and add 1 to updates. Once you’ve done both options for the current (x,y) pair, move on until you’ve covered all y, then all x, then increase i by one and repeat until i reaches n minus 1. When that main loop finishes, you’ll be at layer n in B. Go to the cell at row 0, column 0 of that layer—that’s B[n][0][0]—and read its value. If it’s still INF, set your final result out to -1. Otherwise, out is simply that value. Finally, you return two things: the number out itself, and a little dictionary whose entries are states_processed (the total number of times you saw a finite cell and processed it) and updates (the total number of times you overwrote a cell with a smaller value). 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two pieces. The first is out, a single integer which is either the value from B[n][0][0] if it’s finite or -1 if that cell stayed at INF. The second is a dictionary with two entries: states_processed gives you how many states you actually processed (how often you saw a number that was not INF), and updates tells you how many times you found a smaller cost and updated a cell in the table.
