def f(str1: str, str2: str) -> tuple[int, dict]:
    n = len(str1)
    A = [(int(str2[i]) - int(str1[i])) % 10 for i in range(n)]
    INF = float('inf')
    B = [[[INF] * 10 for _ in range(10)] for __ in range(n + 1)]
    B[0][0][0] = 0
    states_processed = 0
    updates = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for x in range(10):
            for y in range(10):
                c = B[i][x][y]
                if c == INF:
                    continue
                states_processed += 1
                need = (A[i] - x) % 10
                nr = (y + need) % 10
                nl = need
                if B[i + 1][nr][nl] > c + need:
                    B[i + 1][nr][nl] = c + need
                    updates += 1
                dec = (10 - need) % 10
                nr2 = (y - dec) % 10
                nl2 = (-dec) % 10
                if B[i + 1][nr2][nl2] > c + dec:
                    B[i + 1][nr2][nl2] = c + dec
                    updates += 1
    res = B[n][0][0]
    out = res if res < INF else -1
    return out, {"states_processed": states_processed, "updates": updates}

Then create an empty list L. Now look at every pair in A[u] – call each pair (v0, val1). If v0 equals p, just skip it, because that would send you right back where you came from. def f(n, A):
    import heapq
    from collections import Counter
    stats = {'pop_ops': 0, 'push_ops': 0, 'alt_selections': 0}
    mp = Counter(A)
    lst = [(-c, v) for v, c in mp.items()]
    heapq.heapify(lst)
    last = None
    res = 0
    while lst:
        stats['pop_ops'] += 1
        c1, v1 = heapq.heappop(lst)
        c1 = -c1
        if v1 != last:
            last = v1
            c1 -= 1
            if c1 > 0:
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
        else:
            if not lst:
                res += 1
                last = v1
                c1 -= 1
                if c1 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
            else:
                stats['alt_selections'] += 1
                stats['pop_ops'] += 1
                c2, v2 = heapq.heappop(lst)
                c2 = -c2
                last = v2
                c2 -= 1
                heapq.heappush(lst, (-c1, v1))
                stats['push_ops'] += 1
                if c2 > 0:
                    heapq.heappush(lst, (-c2, v2))
                    stats['push_ops'] += 1
    return res, stats

1.  Set a local variable best to zero.  
2.  If i > 0 and j > 0, then add 1 to your rg_ops counter. Look at dp_curr at row i−1, column j−1, take that number and add A’s i-th item (that’s A[i−1]) times B’s j-th item (that’s B[j−1]); call the result v1. If v1 is bigger than best, then replace best with v1.

description:
INPUTS: A is a list of numbers; B is a list of numbers; C is a list of numbers. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is walk through these three lists and build up a running table of scores. First, sort A so the biggest number is first and the smallest is last. Do exactly the same thing with B, and then do it again with C. Next, note down two lengths: call the number of items in A “n” and the number of items in B “m.”

Now set up three counters called rg_ops, rb_ops, and gb_ops, and give each of them a starting value of zero. After that, draw a grid on your paper that has n+1 rows (label them 0 through n) and m+1 columns (label them 0 through m). Fill every cell in that grid with a zero; that whole thing is your dp_prev table.

Here comes the loop over C: take each value x in your sorted C, one at a time, in the order they appear. For each x, you’re going to make a brand-new grid of the same size (n+1 by m+1), fill every cell with zero, and call it dp_curr.

Now the way this works is you will visit every cell in dp_curr by going row by row and column by column. So start with i = 0, then j = 0, then j = 1, all the way up to j = m, then go back to i = 1 and repeat until you reach i = n and j = m. For each pair (i, j), do this:

1.  Set a local variable best to zero.  
2.  If i > 0 and j > 0, then add 1 to your rg_ops counter. Look at dp_curr at row i−1, column j−1, take that number and add A’s i-th item (that’s A[i−1]) times B’s j-th item (that’s B[j−1]); call the result v1. If v1 is bigger than best, then replace best with v1.  
3.  If i > 0, then add 1 to your rb_ops counter. Look at dp_prev at row i−1, column j, take that number and add A’s i-th item (A[i−1]) times x; call it v2. If v2 is bigger than best, replace best with v2.  
4.  If j > 0, then add 1 to your gb_ops counter. Look at dp_prev at row i, column j−1, take that and add B’s j-th item (B[j−1]) times x; call it v3. If v3 is bigger than best, replace best with v3.  
5.  Write best into dp_curr at row i, column j.

Once you’ve done all (i, j) in that dp_curr grid, copy dp_curr over so it becomes the new dp_prev. Then move on to the next x in C and repeat: draw a fresh dp_curr, fill zeros, loop i and j, compute best three ways, update counters, write best, then replace dp_prev.

When you finish the last value in C, dp_prev will be your final grid. The number sitting in row n, column m of that grid is your final output value, and your three counters—rg_ops, rb_ops, and gb_ops—have the totals of how many times you went into each of those three branches during the whole process.

INPUTS: You’re working with three pieces of data. First is n, a single integer that tells you how many items are in your main list. Second is k, another integer that will set how many passes or “strokes” you’ll do. Third is arr, which is a list of n numbers (so arr[0], arr[1], …, arr[n–1]). 

LOGICS: Okay, what you’re going to do is follow these steps exactly:

1. Start by setting two counters:
   - m = 0   (this will count how many times you join things together)
   - y = 0   (this will count how many little DP decisions you make)

2. Handle the tiny‐n case.  Look at n:
   - If n is 0, then you have no items.  In that case your final value val is 0, and both counters m and y stay at 0.  You’re done.
   - If n is 1, then you have exactly one number in arr (that’s arr[0]).  To get val:
       a. Figure out min(k, 0):  if k is negative, min(k, 0) = k; otherwise it’s 0.
       b. Take arr[0], add that min(k, 0), then add k again.  That sum is your val.
     In this n=1 situation you still return m=0 and y=0.  And you stop right there.
   - If n is greater than 1, keep going.

3. Build a helper list L of length n–1.  Write down n–1 zeros to start.
   Now for each index i from 0 up through n–2:
     a. Compute a temporary number x = arr[i] – arr[i+1] + 1.
     b. If x is greater than 0, set L[i] = x; otherwise leave L[i] = 0.
   After you do that, L holds either positive gaps or zeros.

4. Make a bucket structure B of size (k + 2).  In practice you write down k+2 empty lists: B[0], B[1], …, B[k+1].
   Then for each position p from 0 to n–2:
     a. Look at L[p], add 1 to it, call that value x = L[p] + 1.
     b. If x is at least 1 and at most k, go to the list B[x] and append p.
   All the other buckets (B[0], and anything beyond B[k]) stay empty.

5. Set up your union–find structure.  You need two parallel lists of length n:
     A = [0, 1, 2, …, n–1]
     lst = [0, 1, 2, …, n–1]
   A will track parent pointers, and lst will track the smallest original index in each set.

6. Define your find operation.  To find the root of an index x (where x is between 0 and n–1):
     a. While A[x] is not equal to x, do:
          i.   Set A[x] = A[A[x]]   (this flattens the chain)
          ii.  Then set x = A[x]
     b. When you exit the loop, A[x] == x, so return x as the root.

7. Define your union operation on two neighbors u and v:
     a. Let ru = find(u) and rv = find(v).
     b. If ru and rv are the same, do nothing (they’re already joined).
     c. Otherwise:
          i.   Set A[rv] = ru   (attach the second root under the first)
          ii.  If lst[rv] < lst[ru], then set lst[ru] = lst[rv].
          iii. Increment m by 1 (you just made a merge).

8. Prepare a DP list dp1 of length n+1, filled with zeros at indexes 0 through n.

9. Now you do your main loop for stroke from 1 up to k (inclusive).
   For each stroke:
     a. First, look at bucket B[stroke].  For each position p stored in that bucket, call union(p, p+1).  That may update A, lst, and bump up m.
     b. Next, make a fresh list dp2 of length n+1, all zeros.
     c. Then for each i from 1 to n (inclusive), do these steps in order:
          i.   Compute root = find(i–1).  That gives you the representative for index i–1.
          ii.  Compute val = i – lst[root].
          iii. Compute x = dp1[i] + val.
          iv.  Compare dp2[i–1] and x.  If dp2[i–1] is larger, set dp2[i] = dp2[i–1]; otherwise set dp2[i] = x.
          v.   Add 1 to your counter y (that’s one DP step).
     d. After finishing i = 1..n, replace dp1 with dp2 so the next stroke uses the new values.

10. After finishing all strokes from 1 to k, compute your final val.  To do that:
     a. Add up every number in your original list arr to get a sumArr.
     b. Take sumArr and add dp1[n] to it.  That total is your final val.

11. You’re done.  Return two things:
     • val  (the number you just computed in step 10)
     • A dictionary with two entries:
         – 'merges': the final value of m  (how many times you joined two sets)
         – 'dp_steps': the final value of y (how many DP updates you made)
 

OUTPUTS: You end up with a single number val, which is the sum of all elements in arr plus the DP adjustment dp1[n].  Alongside that you get a small dictionary of statistics:

  • 'merges' tells you how many times two items were joined in the union–find process (that’s counter m).
  • 'dp_steps' tells you how many individual DP calculation steps you performed (that’s counter y).

    total=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        total+=B[x]<<x

        return (-1, {"bit_updates": 0, "bit_queries": 0, "bit_searches": 0})
    size=MAXB
    C=[0]*(size+1)
    p=0
    q=0
    r=0
    def D(idx,delta):
        nonlocal p
        p+=1
        while idx<=size:
            C[idx]+=delta
            idx+=idx&-idx
    def E(idx):
        nonlocal q
        q+=1
        m=0
        while idx>0:
            m+=C[idx]
            idx-=idx&-idx
        return m
    def G(target):
        nonlocal r
        r+=1
        pos=0
        bitMask=1<<(size.bit_length())
        while bitMask>0:
            nxt=pos+bitMask
            if nxt<=size and C[nxt]<target:
                target-=C[nxt]
                pos=nxt
            bitMask>>=1
        return pos+1
    for x in range(MAXB):
        if B[x]>0:
            D(x+1,B[x])
    ret=0
    c=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        curr=B[x]+c
        if (k>>x)&1:
            if curr>0:
                curr-=1
            else:

                pos=G(used+1)

                for z in range(y,x,-1):
                    B[z]-=1
                    D(z+1,-1)
                    B[z-1]+=2
                    D(z,2)
                    ret+=1

def f(n,k,A):

    C=[0]*(size+1)
    p=0
    q=0
    r=0
    def D(idx,delta):

        p+=1
        while idx<=size:
            C[idx]+=delta
            idx+=idx&-idx

        nonlocal q
        q+=1
        m=0
        while idx>0:
            m+=C[idx]
            idx-=idx&-idx
        return m

        r+=1
        pos=0
        bitMask=1<<(size.bit_length())
        while bitMask>0:
            nxt=pos+bitMask
            if nxt<=size and C[nxt]<target:
                target-=C[nxt]
                pos=nxt
            bitMask>>=1
        return pos+1
    for x in range(MAXB):
        if B[x]>0:
            D(x+1,B[x])
    ret=0
    c=0
    for x in range(MAXB):
        curr=B[x]+c
        if (k>>x)&1:
            if curr>0:
                curr-=1
            else:
                used=E(x+1)
                pos=G(used+1)
                y=pos-1
                for z in range(y,x,-1):
                    B[z]-=1
                    D(z+1,-1)
                    B[z-1]+=2
                    D(z,2)
                    ret+=1
                curr=B[x]+c
                curr-=1
                B[x]-=1
                D(x+1,-1)
        c=curr//2
    return (ret, {"bit_updates": p, "bit_queries": q, "bit_searches": r})

     • In B[m], append the pair (u, val).
   By the time you finish, A[u] holds all the outward links from u (each as (m, val)), and B[m] holds all the inward links to m (each as (u, val)).

INPUTS: You have a single input called arr, which is just a list of positive whole numbers.  There are no other inputs or settings. 

LOGICS: What you’re going to do is walk through arr step by step and keep track of three little counters along the way.  Here’s how:

1.  Start by figuring out how many items are in arr.  Call that n.  Then create three counters named c1, c2, and c3, and set each one to zero.  These will record your "sieve operations," "factor extractions," and "dp updates" respectively.

2.  Right after that, check if n is 0 or 1.  If it is, you don’t need to do any heavy lifting.  Just stop here and you’ll end up returning 0 plus a dictionary showing c1 = 0, c2 = 0, c3 = 0.

3.  If n is bigger than 1, the next thing is to find the largest number in arr; call it m.  Now build an array called spf of length m + 1 (so its indexes go from 0 up to m), and fill every position with 0.  Think of spf[i] as a place where you’ll store the first prime-like factor you discover for i.

4.  Next you run a loop where i goes from 2 all the way up to m.  For each i:
   - Check spf[i].  If it’s already nonzero, skip it—someone already marked it.
   - If it’s zero, that means i hasn’t been marked yet.  So now start another loop with j = i, then j = i + i, then j = i + 2·i, and so on, as long as j ≤ m.
     * For each of those j values, look at spf[j].  If spf[j] is still zero, set spf[j] = i and add 1 to c1.  If it’s nonzero, leave it alone.  This inner stepping marks every multiple of i exactly once at the moment you first see it.

5.  By the time both loops finish, c1 holds your total "sieve operations."

6.  Now you’re ready to process each number in arr one at a time.  Create an empty map called mp (it starts with no entries) and also set a variable res = 0.

7.  For each item x in arr:
   a. Copy x into a work variable y.  Also make a fresh empty list called L.
   b. While y is bigger than 1:
      – Look up p = spf[y].  That p is your next factor.  Append p onto L, and add 1 to c2 (that’s one more "factor extraction").
      – Now reduce y by dividing out p as many times as you can: while y % p == 0, do y = y // p.  When that inner division loop finishes, go back to the outer while and see if y is still above 1.
   c. At this point L holds a sequence of prime-like factors (with repeats).  Turn L into a set—call it st—so you have each distinct factor just once.
   d. Now figure out where to place x in your hidden sequence by looking at mp.  Set a temporary best = 0, then for each factor p in st:
      – Check mp[p].  If there’s no entry, pretend it’s 0.  If mp[p] is bigger than best, copy mp[p] into best.
   e. Once you’ve scanned all p in st, define dp = best + 1.  If dp is larger than your running res, then update res = dp.
   f. Finally, you update mp for every p in st: if dp is bigger than the current mp[p] (or 0 if none), set mp[p] = dp and add 1 to c3 (that’s one more "dp update").
   g. Move on to the next x in arr and repeat.

8.  When you’ve handled every single x in arr, you’re done.  The number res represents the length of the longest chain you built; the value you actually return is n – res.  Meanwhile c1, c2, c3 hold the counts you collected along the way.
 

OUTPUTS: You come away with two things:

1.  A single number equal to n minus res.  That’s the first part of what you return.
2.  A dictionary with three entries:
   – "sieve_ops": the final value of c1 (how many times you set a new spf entry),
   – "factor_extractions": the final value of c2 (how many times you pulled out a factor p),
   – "dp_updates": the final value of c3 (how many times you updated mp[p]).

LOGICS: What you’re going to do first is set up your workspace with a few counters and an empty list. Start by making a counter called div_ops and set it to zero, another called dp_updates set to zero, and one more called pair_evals set to zero. Then create an empty list called lst.

Next, you need to go through each item in your list A one by one. For each item, which we’ll call val, you’ll figure out two numbers: x and y.

 1. To get x: start by copying val into a temporary variable (let’s call it temp) and set x to zero. Then, while temp is divisible by 2, divide temp by 2 and add 1 to x. Keep doing that until temp is odd. If at any point x becomes greater than m, set x to m and stop dividing by 2 immediately. When you finish, x holds the number of times you divided by 2 (but never more than m).

 2. To get y: start y at zero and copy val into another variable named val2. While val2 is divisible by 5, divide val2 by 5, add 1 to y, and also add 1 to your counter div_ops. Keep going until val2 is no longer divisible by 5 or until y exceeds m. If y goes above m, set y to m and break out of this loop. That way you count every division you actually performed, up to m.

After you’ve determined both x and y for this val, append the pair (x,y) to your list lst. Repeat this process for every element in A—by the end you’ll have lst filled with one (x,y) pair for each original number.

Now you’ll build a two-dimensional tally table M with m+1 rows and m+1 columns, all initialized to zero. You can imagine a grid labeled from row 0 to row m and column 0 to column m, each cell starting at zero. Then go through your list lst again: for each pair (x,y), go to row x, column y in M and add 1 to whatever number is already there. That builds up counts of how many times each combination happened.

Once M is ready, build another table called grid that has one extra row and one extra column—that is, (m+2) by (m+2)—and fill it all with zeros too.

Now comes a filling trick: you’ll traverse grid from bottom-right back to top-left. Concretely, let i go from m down to 0, and inside that let j go from m down to 0. At each cell (i,j), calculate a value by taking M[i][j], adding grid[i+1][j], adding grid[i][j+1], then subtracting grid[i+1][j+1]. Write that result into grid[i][j], and every time you do that add 1 to dp_updates. When you finish all i and j in that reverse order, grid[i][j] tells you how many entries in M lie in the rectangle from (i,j) down to (m,m).

At this point it’s time to compute the final sum. Set a running total res to zero. Then loop i from 0 up to m, and inside that loop j from 0 up to m. For each (i,j) pair:

 - Add 1 to pair_evals.
 - Look at cnt = M[i][j]. If cnt is zero, skip to the next j (nothing to add).
 - Otherwise, compute ri = m - i; if m - i is negative, set ri to 0. Compute rj = m - j; if that is negative, set rj to 0.
 - Look up total_ge = grid[ri][rj]. That number tells you how many (x,y) pairs in M meet or exceed (i,j).
 - Multiply cnt by total_ge and add that to res.
 - Then, if i ≥ ri and j ≥ rj, subtract cnt from res to correct for counting self-pairs twice.

After both loops finish, you’ve counted each pair twice, so divide your running total res by 2. That final quotient is your primary output number.

At the very end, you’ll return two things: first that halved number, and second a small dictionary containing your three counters—div_ops, dp_updates, and pair_evals—so you know how many divisions by 5 you did, how many grid updates you performed, and how many (i,j) pairs you considered in the last step. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with a pair: 1) an integer which is the final summed result divided by two, and 2) a statistics dictionary with three entries: 'div_ops' is the total count of times you divided by 5, 'dp_updates' is the number of times you filled a cell in the reverse-order grid step, and 'pair_evals' is how many (i,j) positions you evaluated in the final nested loops.

def f(n, A, B):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    sz = 4 * n
    tree_s = [0] * sz
    tree_p = [0] * sz
    tree_su = [0] * sz
    tree_m = [0] * sz
    cnt_build = 0
    cnt_query = 0
    cnt_update = 0
    def build(p, l, r):
        nonlocal cnt_build
        cnt_build += 1
        if l == r:
            v = A[l-1]
            tree_s[p] = v
            tree_p[p] = v
            tree_su[p] = v
            tree_m[p] = v
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        build(lc, l, m)
        build(rc, m+1, r)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    def query(p, l, r, i, j):
        nonlocal cnt_query
        cnt_query += 1
        if i <= l and r <= j:
            return tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p]
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if j <= m:
            return query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        if i > m:
            return query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        Ls, Lp, Lsu, Lmx = query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        Rs, Rp, Rsu, Rmx = query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        tot = Ls + Rs
        pre = Lp if Lp > Ls + Rp else Ls + Rp
        suf = Rsu if Rsu > Rs + Lsu else Rs + Lsu
        t1 = Lmx if Lmx > Rmx else Rmx
        mx = t1 if t1 > Lsu + Rp else Lsu + Rp
        return tot, pre, suf, mx
    def update(p, l, r, pos, val):
        nonlocal cnt_update
        cnt_update += 1
        if l == r:
            tree_s[p] = val
            tree_p[p] = val
            tree_su[p] = val
            tree_m[p] = val
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if pos <= m:
            update(lc, l, m, pos, val)
        else:
            update(rc, m+1, r, pos, val)

    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    sz = 4 * n
    tree_s = [0] * sz
    tree_p = [0] * sz
    tree_su = [0] * sz
    tree_m = [0] * sz
    cnt_build = 0
    cnt_query = 0
    cnt_update = 0

        nonlocal cnt_build
        cnt_build += 1

            tree_p[p] = v
            tree_su[p] = v
            tree_m[p] = v
            return

        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs

LOGICS: Start by creating four lists of length four times n, each filled with zeros and call them tree_s, tree_p, tree_su, and tree_m. Also make three counters named cnt_build, cnt_query, and cnt_update and set them all to zero. First you run a build procedure on the entire range from l equal to 1 to r equal to n using a pointer p equal to 1. Each time you enter build you add 1 to cnt_build. Inside build you check if l and r are the same. If they are, you’re at a leaf: grab the value from A at index (l minus one), call it v, and store v into tree_s at p, tree_p at p, tree_su at p, and tree_m at p, then return. If l is not r, compute the midpoint m as floor((l+r)/2), set lc to p times 2 and rc to lc plus 1, then call build on the left child (lc, l, m) and on the right child (rc, m+1, r). When both return, let Ls=tree_s[lc] and Rs=tree_s[rc], then set tree_s[p]=Ls+Rs; set tree_p[p] to the larger of tree_p[lc] and (Ls+tree_p[rc]); set tree_su[p] to the larger of tree_su[rc] and (Rs+tree_su[lc]); to set tree_m[p], first compare tree_m[lc] and tree_m[rc] choose the larger as t1, then choose the larger of t1 and (tree_su[lc]+tree_p[rc]). Return from build. Once that initial sweep is done, create an empty list named res. Now go through each operation triple in B in order: let t be the first number, i the second, j the third. If t equals 1, call an update routine with p=1, l=1, r=n, pos=i, val=j. Inside update add 1 to cnt_update, check if l equals r; if so, overwrite tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p] with j and return; otherwise compute m, lc, rc as before, decide if pos≤m then recurse left else recurse right, then after that recursion finishes recombine tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p] exactly as you did in build, and return. If t equals 2, call a query routine with p=1, l=1, r=n, i, j; inside query add 1 to cnt_query, then check if the segment [l,r] is fully inside [i,j] (i≤l and r≤j) and if so immediately return tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p]. If not, compute m, lc, rc; if j≤m recurse left and return; if i>m recurse right and return; otherwise recurse both: get Ls,Lp,Lsu,Lmx from the left call and Rs,Rp,Rsu,Rmx from the right call, then combine them by setting tot=Ls+Rs, pre=max(Lp, Ls+Rp), suf=max(Rsu, Rs+Lsu), t1=max(Lmx, Rmx), mx=max(t1, Lsu+Rp), and return tot, pre, suf, mx. Back in the main flow for a query, take the fourth returned number, call it ans, and append ans to res. Continue until you process every triple in B. At that point cnt_build tells you how many times you ran build, cnt_query how many times you ran query, and cnt_update how many times you ran update. You then package those three counters into a stats map under keys build_calls, query_calls, and update_calls, and return both res and stats. 

OUTPUTS: You will end up with res, a list of numbers giving each result for the t equals 2 operations in B in order, and a stats map with three entries: build_calls (how many times build ran), query_calls (how many times query ran), and update_calls (how many times update ran).

def f(n, A, B):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    sz = 4 * n
    tree_s = [0] * sz
    tree_p = [0] * sz
    tree_su = [0] * sz
    tree_m = [0] * sz
    cnt_build = 0
    cnt_query = 0
    cnt_update = 0
    def build(p, l, r):
        nonlocal cnt_build
        cnt_build += 1
        if l == r:
            v = A[l-1]
            tree_s[p] = v
            tree_p[p] = v
            tree_su[p] = v
            tree_m[p] = v
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        build(lc, l, m)
        build(rc, m+1, r)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    def query(p, l, r, i, j):
        nonlocal cnt_query
        cnt_query += 1
        if i <= l and r <= j:
            return tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p]
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if j <= m:
            return query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        if i > m:
            return query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        Ls, Lp, Lsu, Lmx = query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        Rs, Rp, Rsu, Rmx = query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        tot = Ls + Rs
        pre = Lp if Lp > Ls + Rp else Ls + Rp
        suf = Rsu if Rsu > Rs + Lsu else Rs + Lsu
        t1 = Lmx if Lmx > Rmx else Rmx
        mx = t1 if t1 > Lsu + Rp else Lsu + Rp
        return tot, pre, suf, mx
    def update(p, l, r, pos, val):
        nonlocal cnt_update
        cnt_update += 1
        if l == r:
            tree_s[p] = val
            tree_p[p] = val
            tree_su[p] = val
            tree_m[p] = val
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if pos <= m:
            update(lc, l, m, pos, val)
        else:
            update(rc, m+1, r, pos, val)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    build(1, 1, n)
    res = []
    for t, i, j in B:
        if t == 1:
            update(1, 1, n, i, j)
        elif t == 2:
            _, _, _, ans = query(1, 1, n, i, j)
            res.append(ans)
    stats = {"build_calls": cnt_build, "query_calls": cnt_query, "update_calls": cnt_update}
    return res, stats

def f(n, A, B):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    sz = 4 * n
    tree_s = [0] * sz
    tree_p = [0] * sz
    tree_su = [0] * sz
    tree_m = [0] * sz
    cnt_build = 0
    cnt_query = 0
    cnt_update = 0
    def build(p, l, r):
        nonlocal cnt_build
        cnt_build += 1
        if l == r:
            v = A[l-1]
            tree_s[p] = v
            tree_p[p] = v
            tree_su[p] = v
            tree_m[p] = v
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        build(lc, l, m)
        build(rc, m+1, r)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    def query(p, l, r, i, j):
        nonlocal cnt_query
        cnt_query += 1
        if i <= l and r <= j:
            return tree_s[p], tree_p[p], tree_su[p], tree_m[p]
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if j <= m:
            return query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        if i > m:
            return query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        Ls, Lp, Lsu, Lmx = query(lc, l, m, i, j)
        Rs, Rp, Rsu, Rmx = query(rc, m+1, r, i, j)
        tot = Ls + Rs
        pre = Lp if Lp > Ls + Rp else Ls + Rp
        suf = Rsu if Rsu > Rs + Lsu else Rs + Lsu
        t1 = Lmx if Lmx > Rmx else Rmx
        mx = t1 if t1 > Lsu + Rp else Lsu + Rp
        return tot, pre, suf, mx
    def update(p, l, r, pos, val):
        nonlocal cnt_update
        cnt_update += 1
        if l == r:
            tree_s[p] = val
            tree_p[p] = val
            tree_su[p] = val
            tree_m[p] = val
            return
        m = (l + r) // 2
        lc = p << 1; rc = lc | 1
        if pos <= m:
            update(lc, l, m, pos, val)
        else:
            update(rc, m+1, r, pos, val)
        Ls, Rs = tree_s[lc], tree_s[rc]
        tree_s[p] = Ls + Rs
        tree_p[p] = tree_p[lc] if tree_p[lc] > Ls + tree_p[rc] else Ls + tree_p[rc]
        tree_su[p] = tree_su[rc] if tree_su[rc] > Rs + tree_su[lc] else Rs + tree_su[lc]
        t1 = tree_m[lc] if tree_m[lc] > tree_m[rc] else tree_m[rc]
        tree_m[p] = t1 if t1 > tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc] else tree_su[lc] + tree_p[rc]
    build(1, 1, n)
    res = []
    for t, i, j in B:
        if t == 1:
            update(1, 1, n, i, j)
        elif t == 2:
            _, _, _, ans = query(1, 1, n, i, j)
            res.append(ans)
    stats = {"build_calls": cnt_build, "query_calls": cnt_query, "update_calls": cnt_update}
    return res, stats

description:
INPUTS: You have three things to start with:

1. n: a single integer. It tells you how many numbered slots you have, from 1 up to n.

2. A: a list of pairs (x, y). Each pair contains two numbers between 1 and n. Think of each pair as a connection from x down to y.

3. B: another list of pairs (x, y). These are the queries you'll process later. Each query involves two numbers between 1 and n, and you’ll keep track of an index for each one. 

LOGICS: Alright, let’s walk through exactly what you’d do by hand. Imagine you’ve got a big sheet of paper and you’re jotting down lists and boxes for each variable.

1. Build L (a list of lists):
   - Write down n + 1 blank lines labeled 0, 1, 2, …, n. You’ll ignore line 0 in practice, but it’s there for convenience.
   - Now go through each pair (x, y) in your list A. For each one, find line x in L and write y on that line. So if A has (3, 5), you go to L[3] and append 5 at the end of whatever’s already there.

2. Build st (a boolean marker list):
   - Make another list of length n+1, fill every entry with the word FALSE.
   - Again go through each pair (x, y) in A. This time, for each y you see, go to st[y] and change it to TRUE. That way you mark every y that ever appears as a second element.

3. Find the root:
   - Look from index 1 up to n in your st list. The very first index i you hit that’s still FALSE is called root. Write down that number as root.

4. Set up your union-find scaffolding:
   - parent: write down numbers 0 through n again. Then put a tick next to each so parent[i] = i for every i from 0 to n.
   - ancestor: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with 0.
   - vis: make a list of length n+1 and fill every slot with FALSE.

5. Build d (a dictionary of adjacency for queries):
   - For each i from 1 to n, start with an empty list d[i].
   - Now go through each query pair in B in order, keeping track of its position idx starting at 0.
     * Suppose the idx-th pair is (x, y). Go to d[x] and append the tuple (y, idx). Then go to d[y] and append the tuple (x, idx).

6. Prepare result and stats containers:
   - res: make a list of length equal to the number of queries in B, and fill it with zeros.
   - stats: make a little table or box with three counters, all starting at 0:
        find_calls = 0
        union_calls = 0
        answered_queries = 0

7. Define your find operation (you won’t really write code, but you’ll follow this logic every time):
   - To "find" u:
     a. Add 1 to your find_calls counter.
     b. Look at parent[u]. If parent[u] is exactly u, you’re done and you return u.
     c. If parent[u] is some other number, say w, then you go and "find(w)" by repeating these steps, and when you get an answer r, you overwrite parent[u] with r. Then you return r.

8. Define your union operation:
   - To "union" u and v:
     a. Add 1 to your union_calls counter.
     b. Find the ultimate parent of v by using your find steps. Call that Pv.
     c. Find the ultimate parent of u by using your find steps. Call that Pu.
     d. Set parent[ Pv ] = Pu. (You attach v’s root under u’s root.)

9. Now do the depth-first sweep starting from root:
   - You’ll write a little note that you’re calling dfs(root).
   - In dfs(u):
     a. First, find the current representative of u by doing find(u). Then go to ancestor[ that representative ] and write down u. In other words, ancestor[ find(u) ] = u.
     b. Next, look at your list L[u]. For each child v in that list, you do:
        i. Call dfs(v) — you repeat all these steps from (a) down for v.
       ii. After dfs(v) finishes, do union(u, v). That merges v’s set into u’s set.
      iii. Right after that union, do ancestor[ find(u) ] = u again, so that the representative for the merged set points to u.
     c. When you’ve done all of u’s children, set vis[u] = TRUE.
     d. Now look at the list d[u]. For every tuple (v, idx) in that list:
        i. Check vis[v]. If vis[v] is still FALSE, skip it and move on.
       ii. If vis[v] is TRUE, then you know you can answer that query now.
           - Add 1 to answered_queries.
           - Find the representative of v by doing find(v), let’s call it Rv.
           - Look up ancestor[Rv], and write that value into res at position idx.
   - That completes dfs(u). When you finish the last line of dfs(root), you’re done with all nodes.

10. Once dfs(root) is fully done, you stop. You haven’t missed any child or any query, because at the moment both vis[u] and vis[v] are TRUE you answered every relevant query exactly once. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll have two things:

1. res – a list of the same length as B. Each entry in res corresponds to one query pair from B (in the same order). The number you see at position idx is exactly the value you wrote into res[idx] during the dfs step when that query was answered.

2. stats – a small dictionary with three numbers:
   • "find_calls": how many times you ran the find operation altogether.  
   • "union_calls": how many times you ran the union operation.  
   • "answered_queries": how many queries from B you actually answered (each time you wrote into res you bumped this by 1).

If i is at least 0 and less than n, and j is at least 0 and less than m, then append j to the sublist A[i]. If either i or j falls outside those bounds, ignore that pair and move on to the next one. At this point youll have A filled with only the in-bounds j’s grouped by their i’s.

After A is ready, set up three more lists in a row: U of length n, V of length m, and D of length n. Fill every slot in U with -1, every slot in V with -1, and every slot in D with 0. That gives you your starting state.

What you do next is define two helper procedures, which well call b and d. These arent functions you run in code—theyre processes you follow by hand.

Helper b:
• Begin by writing down an empty queue. You can represent it as a list where you add items at the end and remove them from the front.  
• Next, go through each index i from 0 up to n–1. If U[i] is -1, set D[i] to 0 and enqueue i. If U[i] is not -1, set D[i] to INF.  
• Write down a flag called found and set it to False.  
• Now, repeat the following until your queue is empty:  
  – Dequeue an index i from the front.  
  – For each j in the list A[i], do:  
    · Add 1 to your counter x (this marks that youve inspected this j during b).  
    · Look at V[j] and call that number w.  
    · If w is not -1 and D[w] is INF, then set D[w] to D[i] + 1 and enqueue w.  
    · Else if w is -1, set found to True (but keep checking other j’s and queue items).  
• When the queue finally empties out, b ends by returning the value of found (True or False).

• If you finish the loop without returning True, set D[i] = INF and return False.

def f(n, k, lst):
    st = set()
    for a, b, _ in lst:
        st.add(a)
        st.add(b + 1)
    arr = sorted(st)
    d = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(arr)}
    m = len(arr)
    if m <= 1:
        return (0, {"update_calls": 0, "push_calls": 0, "pull_calls": 0})
    x = m - 1
    size = 4 * x + 5
    A = [0] * size
    B = [0] * size
    C = [0] * size
    D = [0] * size
    E = [0] * size
    F = [0] * size
    c_u = 0
    c_pu = 0
    c_pl = 0
    def build(node, l, r):
        if l == r:
            F[node] = arr[l + 1] - arr[l]
            return
        mid = (l + r) // 2
        lc = node * 2
        rc = node * 2 + 1
        build(lc, l, mid)
        build(rc, mid + 1, r)
        F[node] = F[lc] + F[rc]
    def apply(node, val):
        A[node] += val
        B[node] += val
    def push(node):
        nonlocal c_pu
        c_pu += 1
        if B[node] != 0:
            v = B[node]
            lc = node * 2
            rc = node * 2 + 1
            apply(lc, v)
            apply(rc, v)
            B[node] = 0
    def pull(node):
        nonlocal c_pl
        c_pl += 1
        lc = node * 2
        rc = node * 2 + 1
        A[node] = A[lc] if A[lc] < A[rc] else A[rc]
        if A[lc] >= k:
            C[node] = F[lc] + C[rc]
        else:
            C[node] = C[lc]
        if A[rc] >= k:
            D[node] = F[rc] + D[lc]
        else:
            D[node] = D[rc]
        v1 = E[lc]
        v2 = E[rc]
        v3 = D[lc] + C[rc]
        t = v1 if v1 > v2 else v2
        E[node] = t if t > v3 else v3
    def update(node, l, r, ql, qr):
        nonlocal c_u
        c_u += 1
        if ql > r or qr < l:
            return
        if ql <= l and r <= qr:
            apply(node, 1)
            return
        push(node)
        mid = (l + r) // 2
        lc = node * 2
        rc = node * 2 + 1
        if ql <= mid:
            update(lc, l, mid, ql, qr)
        if qr > mid:
            update(rc, mid + 1, r, ql, qr)
        pull(node)
    build(1, 0, x - 1)
    lst.sort(key=lambda t: t[2])
    best = 0
    for a, b, w in lst:
        Lc = d[a]
        Rc = d[b + 1] - 1
        if Lc <= Rc:
            update(1, 0, x - 1, Lc, Rc)
        cur = E[1] * w
        if cur > best:
            best = cur
    return (best, {"update_calls": c_u, "push_calls": c_pu, "pull_calls": c_pl})

LOGICS: Start by creating an empty set called st.

Next, go through each item in lst. For each triple, take the first number a and put it into st, then take the second number b and put b+1 into st as well.

After you've done that for every item, gather all numbers from st, sort them into a list called arr.

Now build a dictionary called d: for each position i in arr, set d[arr[i]] = i.

Let m be the length of arr. If m is 1 or less, you have no ranges to handle, so you immediately return (0, {"update_calls": 0, "push_calls": 0, "pull_calls": 0}).

Otherwise, compute x = m - 1, then compute size = 4 * x + 5.

Create six arrays—A, B, C, D, E, F—each of length size, and fill them with zeros.
Also set three counters c_u, c_pu, c_pl all to zero. These will track how many times you invoke update, push, and pull.

What you do next is define a helper called build(node, l, r):
- If l == r, you’re at a leaf segment. Look up arr[l+1] - arr[l], store that difference in F[node], and return.
- Otherwise, compute mid = (l + r) // 2. Let lc = node * 2, rc = node * 2 + 1. First call build(lc, l, mid), then build(rc, mid + 1, r). After both calls finish, set F[node] = F[lc] + F[rc], then return.

Then define apply(node, val):
- Add val to A[node]
- Add val to B[node]

Next, define push(node):
- Increment c_pu by 1
- If B[node] != 0, let v = B[node], set lc = node*2, rc = node*2+1, then call apply(lc, v) and apply(rc, v), and finally set B[node] = 0.

After that, define pull(node):
- Increment c_pl by 1
- Let lc = node*2, rc = node*2+1
- Set A[node] = the smaller of A[lc] and A[rc]
- For C[node]: if A[lc] >= k, set C[node] = F[lc] + C[rc]; otherwise set C[node] = C[lc]
- For D[node]: if A[rc] >= k, set D[node] = F[rc] + D[lc]; otherwise set D[node] = D[rc]
- Compute v1 = E[lc], v2 = E[rc], v3 = D[lc] + C[rc]
- Set E[node] to the largest of v1, v2, and v3

Then define update(node, l, r, ql, qr):
- Increment c_u by 1
- If ql > r or qr < l, there’s no overlap—just return
- If ql <= l and r <= qr, the entire segment is covered: call apply(node, 1) and return
- Otherwise you have a partial overlap:
  - First call push(node)
  - Compute mid = (l + r) // 2, lc = node*2, rc = node*2+1
  - If ql <= mid, call update(lc, l, mid, ql, qr)
  - If qr > mid, call update(rc, mid+1, r, ql, qr)
  - After those calls, call pull(node) and then return

At this point you’ve defined all your helpers. Now call build(1, 0, x - 1) to fill F.

Next, sort lst in ascending order by the third value w.

Initialize a variable best to 0.

Now go through each triple (a, b, w) in the sorted list:
- Look up Lc = d[a]
- Look up Rc = d[b + 1] - 1
- If Lc <= Rc, call update(1, 0, x - 1, Lc, Rc)
- After that, take E[1], multiply it by w to get cur
- If cur > best, set best = cur

Once you’ve processed every item, you’re done with the main processing flow. 

OUTPUTS: When you finish, you’ll return a pair. The first element is best, a single number. The second element is a dictionary with three entries: update_calls (the final value of c_u), push_calls (the final value of c_pu), and pull_calls (the final value of c_pl). These three numbers tell you how many times you ran the update logic, how many times you pushed pending updates down to children, and how many times you pulled or recomputed values back up.

  • Add 1 to stats['group_ops'].

After you finish that loop, you’ll have d1 and d2 mapping values to how many times they appeared in even or odd positions. Now set stats['unique_colors'] to the total number of keys in d1 plus the total number of keys in d2.

Next, convert those dictionaries into lists of pairs: create arr1 as the list of (key, count) pairs from d1, and arr2 as the list of (key, count) pairs from d2.

At this point you want the top two counts from each list. You’ll define a procedure called quickselect_top_k(arr, k):

     – Add 1 to stats['partition_calls'].

INPUTS: You have three inputs: a whole number n, a whole number k, and a text string s of length n made up of digit characters. 

LOGICS: Start by setting two fixed numbers: x equals 9,113,823 and m equals 1,000,000,007. Next create an array A of size n plus one and fill every entry with the value one. Now run through A from index 1 up to index n. At each position i take the value in A at i minus one, multiply it by x, then take the remainder when you divide by m, and store that result in A at position i.  

What you’ve built in A is the sequence of powers of x modulo m.  

Now make another array B of the same size (n plus one) and fill it with zeros. Then for each index i from zero up to n minus one do this:  
1) Compute a small number v by taking the ASCII code of the character s at position i, subtracting the ASCII code of the character zero, then adding one.

INPUTS: You have four inputs:
- n: a single integer that tells you how many items you’re working with,
- arr: a list of n integers,
- lst: another list of n integers,
- edges: a list of pairs of integers, each pair showing two positions that are connected. 

LOGICS: Start by creating a counter dictionary called d with three entries all set to zero: xor_dfs_calls, ans_dfs_calls, and trie_bit_ops. Next, build an adjacency list G by making a list of n empty lists. Now go through each pair (u, v) in edges: subtract 1 from u and from v to switch to zero-based indexing, then append v into G[u] and u into G[v].

Now set up a list called vals of length n and fill it with zeros. Then assign vals[0] = arr[0].

What you’re going to do next is a first depth-first walk to compute a running XOR for each position. Define a procedure called dfs1 that takes a current position u and its parent p. Inside dfs1, the very first thing is to add 1 to d['xor_dfs_calls']. Then look at each neighbor v in G[u]. If v is equal to p, skip it. Otherwise, compute vals[v] = vals[u] XOR arr[v], and then call dfs1(v, u). When you finish all neighbors, return. To kick it off, call dfs1(0, -1).

At this point, vals holds an integer at each index. Next, figure out how many bits you need. Start a variable val = 0. Go through each x in vals; if x is greater than val, set val = x. Then go through each x in lst; if x is greater than val, set val = x. Now val is the maximum integer you’ll see. Compute bits = the number of bits needed to represent val (that is, write val in binary and count its digits).

Next you’ll build a binary trie structure. Define a helper called new_node that returns [count, zero_child, one_child], initially [0, None, None]. Create a root node rt by calling new_node().

Then prepare three helpers:

1. add(x):
   - Set node = rt.
   - For each bit position i from bits-1 down to 0:
     * Add 1 to node[0] and also add 1 to d['trie_bit_ops'].
     * Find the bit bbit = (x >> i) & 1.
     * Look at node[1 + bbit]. If it’s None, replace it with new_node().
     * Then set node = node[1 + bbit].
   - After the loop, add 1 to node[0].

2. remove(x):
   - Do the same steps as add, but subtract 1 from node[0] at each step (and also subtract 1 from node[0] after the loop). Still add 1 to d['trie_bit_ops'] at each bit step.

3. query(x, k):
   - Set node = rt and res_q = 0.
   - For each bit index i from bits-1 down to 0:
     * Add 1 to d['trie_bit_ops'].
     * If node is None, break out early.
     * Compute xb = (x >> i) & 1 and kb = (k >> i) & 1.
     * If kb == 1:
         · Look at child = node[1 + xb]. If child is not None, add child[0] to res_q.
         · Then set node = node[1 + (1 - xb)].
       Else (kb == 0):
         · Set node = node[1 + xb].
   - After the loop, if node is not None, add node[0] to res_q.
   - Return res_q.

Now you’re ready for the second depth-first walk. Create a list res of length n filled with zeros. Define dfs2(u, p) like this:
   1. Add 1 to d['ans_dfs_calls'].
   2. Compute res[u] = query(vals[u], lst[u]).
   3. Call add(vals[u]).
   4. For each neighbor v in G[u], if v is not p, call dfs2(v, u).
   5. After you return from all children, call remove(vals[u]).

Finally, call dfs2(0, -1). After it finishes, you will have filled every entry in res and updated the three counters in d. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two things:
1. res: a list of n integers, where each entry res[u] was computed by querying the trie with vals[u] and lst[u] during the second depth-first walk.
2. d: a dictionary of three counts:
   - xor_dfs_calls: how many times the first dfs1 procedure ran,
   - ans_dfs_calls: how many times the second dfs2 procedure ran,
   - trie_bit_ops: the total number of single-bit steps you performed inside add, remove, and query.

def f(n, m, str1):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    A = [-1] * n
    B = [0] * n
    C = [False] * n
    D = []
    E = [0] * n
    val = 0
    cnt = 0
    rcalls = 0
    curr_depth = 0
    max_depth = 0

    def tarjan(x):
        nonlocal val, cnt, rcalls, curr_depth, max_depth
        rcalls += 1
        curr_depth += 1
        if curr_depth > max_depth:
            max_depth = curr_depth
        try:
            A[x] = val
            B[x] = val
            val += 1
            D.append(x)
            C[x] = True
            y = (x + m) % n
            if A[y] == -1:
                tarjan(y)
                B[x] = B[x] if B[x] < B[y] else B[y]
            elif C[y]:
                B[x] = B[x] if B[x] < A[y] else A[y]
            if B[x] == A[x]:
                while True:
                    z = D.pop()
                    C[z] = False
                    E[z] = cnt
                    if z == x:
                        break
                cnt += 1
        finally:
            curr_depth -= 1

    for x in range(n):
        if A[x] == -1:
            tarjan(x)

    F = [[] for _ in range(cnt)]
    for x in range(n):
        F[E[x]].append(x)

    res = 0
    for G in F:
        mp = {}
        for x in G:
            ch = str1[x]
            mp[ch] = mp.get(ch, 0) + 1
        max_f = max(mp.values())
        res += len(G) - max_f

    stats = {"tarjan_calls": rcalls, "max_recursion_depth": max_depth, "scc_count": cnt}
    return res, stats

def f(n, m, str1):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    A = [-1] * n
    B = [0] * n
    C = [False] * n
    D = []
    E = [0] * n
    val = 0
    cnt = 0
    rcalls = 0
    curr_depth = 0
    max_depth = 0

    def tarjan(x):
        nonlocal val, cnt, rcalls, curr_depth, max_depth
        rcalls += 1
        curr_depth += 1
        if curr_depth > max_depth:
            max_depth = curr_depth
        try:
            A[x] = val
            B[x] = val
            val += 1
            D.append(x)
            C[x] = True
            y = (x + m) % n
            if A[y] == -1:
                tarjan(y)
                B[x] = B[x] if B[x] < B[y] else B[y]
            elif C[y]:
                B[x] = B[x] if B[x] < A[y] else A[y]
            if B[x] == A[x]:
                while True:
                    z = D.pop()
                    C[z] = False
                    E[z] = cnt
                    if z == x:
                        break
                cnt += 1
        finally:
            curr_depth -= 1

    for x in range(n):

def f(n, m, str1):
    import sys
    sys.setrecursionlimit(10**7)
    A = [-1] * n
    B = [0] * n
    C = [False] * n
    D = []
    E = [0] * n
    val = 0
    cnt = 0
    rcalls = 0
    curr_depth = 0
    max_depth = 0

    def tarjan(x):
        nonlocal val, cnt, rcalls, curr_depth, max_depth
        rcalls += 1
        curr_depth += 1
        if curr_depth > max_depth:
            max_depth = curr_depth
        try:
            A[x] = val
            B[x] = val
            val += 1
            D.append(x)
            C[x] = True
            y = (x + m) % n
            if A[y] == -1:
                tarjan(y)
                B[x] = B[x] if B[x] < B[y] else B[y]
            elif C[y]:
                B[x] = B[x] if B[x] < A[y] else A[y]
            if B[x] == A[x]:
                while True:
                    z = D.pop()
                    C[z] = False
                    E[z] = cnt
                    if z == x:
                        break
                cnt += 1
        finally:
            curr_depth -= 1

    for x in range(n):
        if A[x] == -1:
            tarjan(x)

    F = [[] for _ in range(cnt)]
    for x in range(n):
        F[E[x]].append(x)

    res = 0
    for G in F:
        mp = {}
        for x in G:
            ch = str1[x]
            mp[ch] = mp.get(ch, 0) + 1
        max_f = max(mp.values())
        res += len(G) - max_f

    stats = {"tarjan_calls": rcalls, "max_recursion_depth": max_depth, "scc_count": cnt}
    return res, stats

def f(n, arr, A, B):
    from heapq import heapify, heappush, heappop
    L = sorted(range(n), key=lambda x: arr[x])
    P = [-1] * n
    N = [-1] * n
    for idx, i in enumerate(L):
        if idx > 0:
            P[i] = L[idx - 1]
        if idx < n - 1:
            N[i] = L[idx + 1]
    lst = A[:]
    pr = [-1] * n
    seen = [False] * n
    pq = [(lst[i], i) for i in range(n)]
    heapify(pq)
    total = 0
    out1 = []
    out2 = []
    push_count = 0
    pop_count = 0
    check_count = 0
    while pq:
        cost, i = heappop(pq)
        pop_count += 1
        if seen[i]:
            continue
        seen[i] = True
        total += cost
        if pr[i] == -1:
            out1.append(i + 1)
        else:
            out2.append((pr[i] + 1, i + 1))
        p = P[i]
        q = N[i]
        if p != -1:
            N[p] = q
        if q != -1:
            P[q] = p
        j = p
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = P[j]
            else:
                break
        j = q
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1

def f(n, arr, A, B):
    from heapq import heapify, heappush, heappop
    L = sorted(range(n), key=lambda x: arr[x])
    P = [-1] * n
    N = [-1] * n
    for idx, i in enumerate(L):
        if idx > 0:
            P[i] = L[idx - 1]
        if idx < n - 1:
            N[i] = L[idx + 1]
    lst = A[:]
    pr = [-1] * n
    seen = [False] * n
    pq = [(lst[i], i) for i in range(n)]
    heapify(pq)
    total = 0
    out1 = []
    out2 = []
    push_count = 0
    pop_count = 0
    check_count = 0
    while pq:
        cost, i = heappop(pq)
        pop_count += 1
        if seen[i]:
            continue
        seen[i] = True
        total += cost
        if pr[i] == -1:
            out1.append(i + 1)
        else:
            out2.append((pr[i] + 1, i + 1))
        p = P[i]
        q = N[i]
        if p != -1:
            N[p] = q
        if q != -1:
            P[q] = p
        j = p
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = P[j]
            else:
                break
        j = q
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = N[j]
            else:
                break
    return ((total, out1, out2), {'heap_pushes': push_count, 'heap_pops': pop_count, 'neighbor_checks': check_count})

def f(n, arr, A, B):
    from heapq import heapify, heappush, heappop
    L = sorted(range(n), key=lambda x: arr[x])
    P = [-1] * n
    N = [-1] * n
    for idx, i in enumerate(L):
        if idx > 0:
            P[i] = L[idx - 1]
        if idx < n - 1:
            N[i] = L[idx + 1]
    lst = A[:]
    pr = [-1] * n
    seen = [False] * n
    pq = [(lst[i], i) for i in range(n)]
    heapify(pq)
    total = 0
    out1 = []
    out2 = []
    push_count = 0
    pop_count = 0
    check_count = 0
    while pq:
        cost, i = heappop(pq)
        pop_count += 1
        if seen[i]:
            continue
        seen[i] = True
        total += cost
        if pr[i] == -1:
            out1.append(i + 1)
        else:
            out2.append((pr[i] + 1, i + 1))
        p = P[i]
        q = N[i]
        if p != -1:
            N[p] = q
        if q != -1:
            P[q] = p
        j = p
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = P[j]
            else:
                break
        j = q
        while j != -1:
            check_count += 1
            val = (B[i] + B[j]) * abs(arr[i] - arr[j])
            if val < lst[j]:
                lst[j] = val
                pr[j] = i
                heappush(pq, (val, j))
                push_count += 1
                j = N[j]
            else:
                break
    return ((total, out1, out2), {'heap_pushes': push_count, 'heap_pops': pop_count, 'neighbor_checks': check_count})

def f(x, lst):
    B = []
    nonone_window_iterations = 0
    pure_one_cases = 0
    one_block_segments = 0
    for d in lst:
        n = d['n']
        y = d['k']
        A = d['a']
        L = [i for i,v in enumerate(A) if v != 1]
        m = len(L)
        val = 0
        if m == 0:
            pure_one_cases += 1
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val = n * (n - 1) // 2
            else:
                val = n * (n + 1) // 2
            B.append(val)
            continue
        LOG = 60
        for i in range(m):
            p = 1
            s = 0
            for j in range(i, min(m, i + LOG)):
                nonone_window_iterations += 1
                idx = L[j]
                v = A[idx]
                p *= v
                s += v
                l = L[i] - (L[i - 1] if i > 0 else -1) - 1
                r = (L[j + 1] if j + 1 < m else n) - idx - 1
                req = (p + y) // y - s
                if req > l + r:
                    continue
                total = (l + 1) * (r + 1)
                if req <= 0:
                    val += total
                else:
                    bad = 0
                    ml = min(l, req - 1)
                    for uu in range(ml + 1):
                        rm = req - 1 - uu
                        bad += min(r, rm) + 1
                    val += total - bad
        pr = -1
        for idx in L:
            gap = idx - pr - 1
            if gap > 0:
                one_block_segments += 1
                if y == 1:
                    val += gap * (gap - 1) // 2
                else:
                    val += gap * (gap + 1) // 2
            pr = idx
        tail = n - L[-1] - 1
        if tail > 0:
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val += tail * (tail - 1) // 2
            else:
                val += tail * (tail + 1) // 2
        B.append(val)
    return B, {'nonone_window_iterations': nonone_window_iterations, 'pure_one_cases': pure_one_cases, 'one_block_segments': one_block_segments}

    nonone_window_iterations = 0
    pure_one_cases = 0
    one_block_segments = 0
    for d in lst:

        y = d['k']
        A = d['a']
        L = [i for i,v in enumerate(A) if v != 1]
        m = len(L)
        val = 0
        if m == 0:
            pure_one_cases += 1
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val = n * (n - 1) // 2
            else:
                val = n * (n + 1) // 2
            B.append(val)
            continue
        LOG = 60
        for i in range(m):

    return B, {'nonone_window_iterations': nonone_window_iterations, 'pure_one_cases': pure_one_cases, 'one_block_segments': one_block_segments}

def f(x, lst):
    B = []
    nonone_window_iterations = 0
    pure_one_cases = 0
    one_block_segments = 0
    for d in lst:
        n = d['n']
        y = d['k']
        A = d['a']
        L = [i for i,v in enumerate(A) if v != 1]
        m = len(L)
        val = 0
        if m == 0:
            pure_one_cases += 1
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val = n * (n - 1) // 2
            else:
                val = n * (n + 1) // 2
            B.append(val)
            continue
        LOG = 60
        for i in range(m):
            p = 1
            s = 0
            for j in range(i, min(m, i + LOG)):
                nonone_window_iterations += 1
                idx = L[j]

                    val += total

                    ml = min(l, req - 1)

                val += tail * (tail + 1) // 2
        B.append(val)
    return B, {'nonone_window_iterations': nonone_window_iterations, 'pure_one_cases': pure_one_cases, 'one_block_segments': one_block_segments}

        y = d['k']

        L = [i for i,v in enumerate(A) if v != 1]
        m = len(L)
        val = 0
        if m == 0:
            pure_one_cases += 1
            one_block_segments += 1
            if y == 1:
                val = n * (n - 1) // 2
            else:
                val = n * (n + 1) // 2
            B.append(val)
            continue

Next, set n equal to the number of pairs in A. Then you build a new list called B, also of length n: go through each pair in A, call the two numbers x and y, compute the arctan2 of y and x, and store that angle in B at the same position. After you have B, create a list called arr that just contains the indices from 0 up to n–1, but sorted so that B[arr[0]] is the smallest angle, B[arr[1]] the next smallest, and so on. Now make a list C by taking the elements of A in the order given by arr (so C[i] = A[arr[i]]). Then build D by sticking two copies of C back-to-back (so D has length m = 2·n). At this point, create an m×m table called M and fill every entry with 0. Also set three counters, c1, c2, and c3, all to zero. Now fill in M’s upper triangle: for i from 0 to m−1, let (x1,y1) = D[i]; then for j from i+1 to m−1, let (x2,y2) = D[j], compute a value by doing x1×y2 minus y1×x2, store that result in M[i][j], and add 1 to c1. After those loops finish, set a variable val_max to 0. Now you begin a sliding‐window phase: for each start index s from 0 to n−1, compute end = s + n. Create a list lst_prev of length m and fill every slot with negative infinity. Then for j from s+1 to end−1, set lst_prev[j] = M[s][j]. That seeds your first stage. INPUTS: You start with two integers and a grid of characters. n is the number of rows, m is the number of columns, and M is a list of n lists, each of length m, where each entry is a single character (either '*' or something else). 

LOGICS: First, what you're going to do is set up your workspace by creating four new n-by-m matrices filled with zeros, and you’ll call them M1, M2, M3, and M4. At the same time, make a stats dictionary with three counters—all set to zero—named 'dp_updates', 'center_evaluations', and 'verify_checks'.

Now you need to fill M1 and M2 in one sweep. So you go row by row: for each i from 0 up to n minus 1, and for each j from 0 up to m minus 1, check if M[i][j] is '*'. If it is, compute M1[i][j] by taking 1 plus the value at M1[i-1][j] if i is greater than 0, otherwise just use 1. As soon as you fill M1[i][j], add 1 to stats['dp_updates']. Then compute M2[i][j] by taking 1 plus M2[i][j-1] if j is greater than 0, otherwise 1, and again add 1 to stats['dp_updates'].

Once that top-left to bottom-right pass is done, you do a second pass backward to fill M3 and M4. Loop i from n minus 1 down to 0, and inside that loop j from m minus 1 down to 0. Whenever you see M[i][j] is '*', compute M3[i][j] as 1 plus M3[i+1][j] if i is less than n minus 1, otherwise 1, then add 1 to stats['dp_updates']. Next compute M4[i][j] as 1 plus M4[i][j+1] if j is less than m minus 1, otherwise 1, and add another 1 to stats['dp_updates'].

At this point you have four direction‐counts for every star. Now you want to find the best candidate center. So set max_val to 0 and x and y to -1. Then scan every cell again (i from 0 to n minus 1, j from 0 to m minus 1). If M[i][j] is '*', add 1 to stats['center_evaluations'], then look at the four numbers M1[i][j], M3[i][j], M2[i][j], and M4[i][j] and take the minimum—call that cur_val. If cur_val is bigger than max_val, update max_val to cur_val and record x = i, y = j.

After you finish that search, check if max_val is less than or equal to 1. If it is, you immediately stop and return 'NO' along with your stats, because you didn’t find a large enough shape.

If max_val is greater than 1, you build a boolean matrix B of size n by m all set to False. Then set B[x][y] = True. Compute r as max_val minus 1. For each k from 1 to r inclusive, set B[x-k][y] = True, B[x+k][y] = True, B[x][y-k] = True, and B[x][y+k] = True. That marks out a symmetric pattern around the chosen center.

Finally, you verify that every '*' in M falls onto a True spot in B. So you loop i and j over all positions again; whenever M[i][j] is '*', add 1 to stats['verify_checks'], then check if B[i][j] is True. If you ever find a '*' where B[i][j] is False, you return 'NO' and your stats. If you get through that entire check without failing, you return 'YES' and the stats. 

OUTPUTS: You end up with two items: a string that is either 'YES' or 'NO', and the stats dictionary. In stats, 'dp_updates' is the total count of times you wrote into any of M1, M2, M3, or M4; 'center_evaluations' is the number of starred cells you tested as potential centers; and 'verify_checks' is the number of starred cells you rechecked against the final pattern.

At this point you define a helper process g that sorts a list of numbers in descending order while counting how many times you compare two numbers. Here’s how g works: if the incoming list arr has length 0 or 1, you just return it immediately. Otherwise find the midpoint m by taking the length of arr, dividing by two, and rounding down. Split arr into two parts— the first m items and the remaining items— then call g on each part to get two sorted sublists A and B. Now you merge A and B by setting two pointers x=0 and y=0 and building a new empty list C. While x is still inside A and y is still inside B, compare A[x] to B[y] and add 1 to sort_comp for that comparison. If A[x] is larger, append A[x] to C and bump x by 1; otherwise append B[y] and bump y by 1. Once one side runs out, append whatever is left of the other side onto C, and then return C.

def f(n, t_lim, L, A):
    B = list(zip(L, A))
    B.append((0, 0))
    B.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    arr = [x[0] for x in B]
    val = [x[1] for x in B]
    m = len(B)
    s = arr.index(0)
    ps = [0] * m
    ps[0] = val[0]
    prefix_sum_ops = 0
    for i in range(1, m):
        ps[i] = ps[i-1] + val[i]
        prefix_sum_ops += 1
    INF = float('inf')
    dp = [[[INF, INF] for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    dp[s][s] = [0, 0]
    ans = 0
    reachable_states = 0
    dp_transitions = 0
    for w in range(m):
        for i in range(s-w, s+1):
            j = i + w
            if i < 0 or j >= m:
                continue
            if dp[i][j][0] == INF and dp[i][j][1] == INF:
                continue
            reachable_states += 1
            total = ps[j] - (ps[i-1] if i > 0 else 0)
            tL = dp[i][j][0] + abs(arr[i])
            if tL <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            tR = dp[i][j][1] + abs(arr[j])
            if tR <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            if i > 0:
                lm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[i] - arr[i-1]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j] - arr[i-1])
                )
                if lm < dp[i-1][j][0]:
                    dp[i-1][j][0] = lm
                    dp_transitions += 1
            if j < m-1:
                rm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[j+1] - arr[i]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j+1] - arr[j])
                )
                if rm < dp[i][j+1][1]:
                    dp[i][j+1][1] = rm
                    dp_transitions += 1
    return ans, {"prefix_sum_ops": prefix_sum_ops, "reachable_states": reachable_states, "dp_transitions": dp_transitions}

def f(n, t_lim, L, A):
    B = list(zip(L, A))
    B.append((0, 0))
    B.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    arr = [x[0] for x in B]
    val = [x[1] for x in B]
    m = len(B)
    s = arr.index(0)
    ps = [0] * m
    ps[0] = val[0]
    prefix_sum_ops = 0
    for i in range(1, m):
        ps[i] = ps[i-1] + val[i]
        prefix_sum_ops += 1
    INF = float('inf')
    dp = [[[INF, INF] for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    dp[s][s] = [0, 0]
    ans = 0
    reachable_states = 0
    dp_transitions = 0
    for w in range(m):
        for i in range(s-w, s+1):
            j = i + w
            if i < 0 or j >= m:
                continue
            if dp[i][j][0] == INF and dp[i][j][1] == INF:
                continue
            reachable_states += 1
            total = ps[j] - (ps[i-1] if i > 0 else 0)
            tL = dp[i][j][0] + abs(arr[i])
            if tL <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            tR = dp[i][j][1] + abs(arr[j])
            if tR <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            if i > 0:
                lm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[i] - arr[i-1]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j] - arr[i-1])
                )
                if lm < dp[i-1][j][0]:
                    dp[i-1][j][0] = lm
                    dp_transitions += 1
            if j < m-1:
                rm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[j+1] - arr[i]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j+1] - arr[j])
                )
                if rm < dp[i][j+1][1]:
                    dp[i][j+1][1] = rm
                    dp_transitions += 1
    return ans, {"prefix_sum_ops": prefix_sum_ops, "reachable_states": reachable_states, "dp_transitions": dp_transitions}

def f(n, t_lim, L, A):
    B = list(zip(L, A))
    B.append((0, 0))
    B.sort(key=lambda x: x[0])
    arr = [x[0] for x in B]
    val = [x[1] for x in B]
    m = len(B)
    s = arr.index(0)
    ps = [0] * m
    ps[0] = val[0]
    prefix_sum_ops = 0
    for i in range(1, m):
        ps[i] = ps[i-1] + val[i]
        prefix_sum_ops += 1
    INF = float('inf')
    dp = [[[INF, INF] for _ in range(m)] for _ in range(m)]
    dp[s][s] = [0, 0]
    ans = 0
    reachable_states = 0
    dp_transitions = 0
    for w in range(m):
        for i in range(s-w, s+1):
            j = i + w
            if i < 0 or j >= m:
                continue
            if dp[i][j][0] == INF and dp[i][j][1] == INF:
                continue
            reachable_states += 1
            total = ps[j] - (ps[i-1] if i > 0 else 0)
            tL = dp[i][j][0] + abs(arr[i])
            if tL <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            tR = dp[i][j][1] + abs(arr[j])
            if tR <= t_lim:
                ans = max(ans, total)
            if i > 0:
                lm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[i] - arr[i-1]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j] - arr[i-1])
                )
                if lm < dp[i-1][j][0]:
                    dp[i-1][j][0] = lm
                    dp_transitions += 1
            if j < m-1:
                rm = min(
                    dp[i][j][0] + (arr[j+1] - arr[i]),
                    dp[i][j][1] + (arr[j+1] - arr[j])
                )
                if rm < dp[i][j+1][1]:
                    dp[i][j+1][1] = rm
                    dp_transitions += 1
    return ans, {"prefix_sum_ops": prefix_sum_ops, "reachable_states": reachable_states, "dp_transitions": dp_transitions}

  - a map called mp, where you'll store parent links for each item,
  - a map called mp2, which will track a rank number for each item,
  - a map called d, which will count how many times each item appears as the second entry in a pair,
  - a set called st, which will keep track of all the distinct items you see,
  - a flag called flag, and set it to False.

Next, go through each pair in A. For each pair, pull out x and y. Add x and y into the set st. If x is not yet a key in mp, put mp[x] = x; do the same for y. If x is not yet in mp2, set mp2[x] = 0; same for y. If x is not yet in d, set d[x] = 0; same for y.

What you do now is define two helper procedures in your head that you’ll apply by hand:
  1. find(a):
     - Each time you call this, add 1 to your find_calls counter.
     - Look at mp[a]. If mp[a] equals a, that means it’s its own parent, so return a.
     - Otherwise, call find(mp[a]) to get the ultimate parent, then set mp[a] to that returned parent (path compression), and then return that parent.

  2. union(a, b):
     - Each time you call this, add 1 to your union_calls counter.
     - Call find(a) and find(b) to get their roots ra and rb.
     - If ra and rb are the same, return False (they’re already connected).
     - Otherwise, compare mp2[ra] and mp2[rb]. If mp2[ra] < mp2[rb], set mp[ra] = rb. Otherwise, set mp[rb] = ra; and if mp2[ra] and mp2[rb] were equal before, add 1 to mp2[ra]. Then return True.

At this point, go back and do another pass over each pair x, y in A in order. For each pair:
  - Add 1 to d[y].

     - Add 1 to connectivity_checks.
     - Call find(n). If that result does not match your chosen root, set flag = True and stop checking.

After that, append (not flag) to your res list—that will be True if none of the checks set flag to True, or False if any check did.

Repeat this entire process for each sublist A inside your original list L. When you’ve processed every A, you’ll have your res list and your three counters populated.

INPUTS: You have two integers: n (the number of rows) and m (the number of columns). Then you have grid, which is a list of n text strings; each string is exactly m characters long and consists only of the characters '0' and '1'. 

LOGICS: Okay, let’s walk through every step so you could literally do this by hand:

1. First off, fix your random number sequence by setting the seed to 0. That way, whenever you pick random numbers later, you’ll get the same sequence.

2. Now you need to build a list called L. What you do is go through each row of grid in order (from row 0 up to row n–1). For each row, scan its characters from column 0 to column m–1. Whenever you see a '1', note down that column index in a small list. After you’ve scanned the whole row, that small list holds exactly the positions of '1's in that row. Do this for every row and collect all those small lists into L. In the end, L is a list of n lists, and each inner list tells you which columns had '1's in that row.

3. Next, set up your working variables:
   – Make a string res of length m that’s all '0's (just write down m zeros in a row).
   – Set v = 0. This will track the size of the best pattern you’ve found so far.
   – Compute thr by taking n plus 1, then dividing by 2 using integer division (ignore any remainder).
   – Let t be the smaller of n and 15.
   – Initialize three counters c1, c2, c3 all to 0. You’ll use them to collect some statistics as you go.

4. Now you’re ready for the main loop. You’re going to repeat the following exactly t times:
   a. Pick a random integer x between 0 and n–1 (inclusive) using your seeded random generator.
   b. Look up P = L[x], and let k = the number of items in P.
   c. If k is not greater than v, skip the rest of this pass and move on to the next repetition.
   d. If k is greater than 20, also skip the rest of this pass and move on.
   e. If you didn’t skip, you’re processing this P as a pivot set, so add 1 to c1.
   f. Now build a map mp from integer masks to counts:
      • Start mp empty.
      • For each arr in L:
         – Convert arr into a set st (so you can check membership quickly).
         – Start an integer val = 0.
         – For each index i from 0 to k–1, look at the column y = P[i]. If y is in st, then set bit i of val by adding 2^i.
         – Once you’ve checked all i’s, increase mp[val] by 1 (if val wasn’t there before, set mp[val] = 1; otherwise add 1).
   g. After you’ve done that for every arr, compute size = 2^k, and make a list B of length size, all zeros.
   h. For each entry (mask, count) in mp, set B[mask] = count.
   i. Now perform the subset‐sum (zeta) pass:
      • For each i from 0 to k–1,
      •   for each s from 0 to size–1,
      •     if the i-th bit of s is 0 (that is, (s & (1<<i)) == 0), then add B[s | (1<<i)] into B[s] and add 1 to c2.
   j. At this point, B[s] tells you how many rows have at least the bits in s. Next, you scan s from 0 to size–1:
      • For each s, add 1 to c3.
      • If B[s] is at least thr, then count how many bits are set in s (call that pop).
      • If pop is greater than v, you’ve got a better pattern:
         – Set v = pop.
         – Make a fresh list C of length m filled with '0'.
         – For each i from 0 to k–1, if bit i of s is 1, set C[P[i]] = '1'.
         – Join C into a string and replace res with that string.
   That completes one of the t passes.

5. After you’ve repeated that entire sequence t times, you’re done with processing. 

OUTPUTS: When all that is finished, you end up with two things:

1. res: a text string of length m made up of '0's and '1's, reflecting the best pattern you found.
2. A dictionary of three counts:
   • 'pivots_processed': c1 — how many pivot lists P you actually processed (i.e. passed both k>v and k≤20 checks).
   • 'zeta_ops': c2 — how many times you performed that subset‐sum addition step in the zeta transform.
   • 'mask_checks': c3 — how many total mask patterns s you inspected in the final scan.

Then you build a structure called grid that has n+1 slots (we ignore slot zero), and for slots 1 through n you make a matrix of size (m+1) by (m+1) and fill every entry with INF. Right after that, you create an empty dictionary mp that will let you trace steps later. Now you initialize your first layer: loop p from 0 up to m. For each p compute q = arr[0] – p. If q sits between 0 and m (inclusive), then set grid[1][p][q] = p + q, record mp[(1, p, q)] = None, and add 1 to your counter x1. Next, you perform the main nested loops: for each i running from 1 up to n-2 inclusive, for each u from 0 to m, and for each v from 0 to m, look at the current value val = grid[i][u][v]. If val is still less than INF, compute w = arr[i] – u – v. If w is between 0 and m inclusive, compute new_val = val + w. Then check if new_val is strictly less than grid[i+1][v][w]. If it is, you overwrite grid[i+1][v][w] with new_val, record mp[(i+1, v, w)] = (i, u, v), and add 1 to x2. Once all those loops finish, you search for the best end state by setting a variable val back to INF, a variable t to None, and letting l = n - 1. If it's smaller, update val to that and t to the triple (l, u, v). When that search is done, if t is still None it means no valid configuration was found, so you return ret = (-1, []) along with {'init_states': x1, 'dp_updates': x2, 'output_len': 0}. If t is not None, you reconstruct the solution path: start by making a list L of length n filled with zeros, and an empty list B.
